text: The results of the three experiments are presented and discussed in this chapter. Experiment I deals with the influence of production location and storage period on the grain quality of three aromatic landraces; Experiment II with the quality of seven processed and cooked products prepared from ten cultivars; and Experiment III with the sensory and nutritional quality of plain and vegetable-fortified idli. All tables and figures in this chapter are numbered continuously in the series 4.1 onwards.

This experiment measured how the place of growing, the landrace and the length of storage after harvest affect the grain quality of three traditional aromatic rices of West Bengal. The landraces were Gobindabhog (V1), Radhunipagal (V2) and Kalojira (V3). They were collected from Nadia (L1), Purba Bardhaman (L2) and Birbhum/Howrah (L3). Each lot was tested as fresh paddy (S1) and again at 4 months (S2), 8 months (S3) and 12 months (S4) after harvest. All lots were stored at Bidhan Chandra Krishi Viswavidyalaya, Mohanpur, under the same ambient conditions, so that location refers to the place of growing only. The design was a factorial randomised block design with three replications. The trial was repeated in 2022–23 and 2023–24. Thirty-eight parameters were recorded. They are presented under seven headings: physical, sensory, nutritional, anti-nutritional, colour, minerals and amino acids. Data were analysed by analysis of variance for a three-factor factorial randomised block design (Das and Giri, 1986). Year was included as an additional factor. The year × treatment interactions were non-significant for most parameters. All means reported below are therefore pooled over the two years. SEm, CD at the 5% level and CV were computed from the pooled error mean square with 140 degrees of freedom. Means sharing a common letter do not differ at the 5% level by the least significant difference test. In the tables GB, RP and KJ denote the three landraces in the order given above. Amino acids were assayed on freshly harvested grain alone. Section 4.7 therefore reports S1 means only and no effect of storage.

The three locations gave different values of hulling, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 77.02% was recorded at Nadia. Purba Bardhaman came next with 75.59% and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 75.28%. No two locations shared a letter group. Every location stood apart from the other two. The best and poorest locations differed by 1.73 percentage points.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 77.52%, followed by Gobindabhog with 75.78% and Radhunipagal with 74.58%. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 2.94 percentage points.

Storage changed hulling. The effect reached the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 76.82% in fresh paddy, 76.92% at 4 months, 74.30% at 8 months and 75.81% at 12 months. Across the twelve months the value dropped by 1.3%. The highest value came from 4 months and the lowest from 8 months.

The location by variety interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Nadia with 78.55%. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah with 73.99%. The three landraces kept the same order at each location. The sequence was Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal. The interaction altered how large the varietal differences were, not which way they ran.

Location and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 78.89% for Nadia at 4 months. The lowest was 73.81% for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. From fresh paddy to 12 months the value shifted -1.3% at Nadia, -1.2% at Purba Bardhaman and -1.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. The change was of similar magnitude at all three locations. Storage, which took place at a single site, affected grain from every location similarly.

Variety and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 79.01% for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 73.45% for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Across twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -0.7%, Radhunipagal by -1.3% and Kalojira by -2.0%. The three landraces shifted by close to equal amounts. Storage affected all three similarly.

The three-way interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 80.20% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months. The lowest value of 72.38% came from Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months. The spread between these two cells was 7.82 percentage points. That range far exceeds the spread produced by any one factor alone. The three factors worked jointly. A good result therefore needs all three set correctly.

Hulling expresses the proportion of brown rice obtained when the husk is removed. The three locations gave different values, which shows that where the crop is grown matters. Li et al. (2018) found that temperature, sunlight and humidity in the weeks after flowering affect milling outturn more than most other quality traits. Singh et al. (2000) and Mahendra et al. (2019) reported a similar difference among small and medium grained Indian aromatic rices, and Patra et al. (2024) recorded hulling of 77.6 to 77.9% in the West Bengal aromatic landrace Tulaipanji, which is close to the figure obtained for Kalojira here. Wongpornchai et al. (2004) and Zhou et al. (2002) also linked milling behaviour to the moisture state of the grain rather than to any lasting chemical change, and Müller et al. (2022) concluded from a wide review of post-harvest work that keeping stored grain in hygroscopic balance is the single most important factor in preserving milling quality.

The three locations gave different values of milling, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 71.38% was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 70.30% and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 68.99%. The three locations separated into distinct groups. The three locations all differed from one another. A margin of 2.39 percentage points separated the best location from the worst.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 71.63%, followed by Gobindabhog with 70.87% and Radhunipagal with 68.17%. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 3.47 percentage points.

Storage changed milling. This effect was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 70.21% in fresh paddy, 71.49% at 4 months, 68.62% at 8 months and 70.56% at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 0.5%. The highest value came from 4 months and the lowest from 8 months.

Location and variety interacted significantly at the 1% level. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 72.89%. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 66.90%. Landrace order was unchanged from one location to the next. It went Kalojira, then Gobindabhog, then Radhunipagal. What the interaction changed was the magnitude of the varietal gap, not its sign.

No significant interaction arose between location and storage. The highest mean was 72.69% for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months. The lowest was 67.55% for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +0.6% at Nadia, +0.8% at Purba Bardhaman, +0.2% at Birbhum/Howrah. All three locations moved by close to the same amount. The effect of storage was the same whatever the district of origin.

No significant interaction appeared between variety and storage. The highest mean was 72.94% for Kalojira at 4 months. The lowest was 66.42% for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Over the twelve months the change was +0.2% in Gobindabhog, +0.3% in Radhunipagal, +1.0% in Kalojira. All three changed by similar amounts. The landraces responded to storage in the same way.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 73.88% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 4 months. The lowest value of 65.21% came from Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Milling percentage is the weight of polished rice left from the original paddy. It is the figure that decides how much a miller earns from a given lot, so it carries direct commercial weight. Milling recovery depends on how firmly the endosperm is packed, and that is settled by the weather during grain filling. Tsado et al. (2015) found that grain cracking and breakage in milled rice depend strongly on the cultivar and deteriorate as paddy is stored for longer. Müller et al. (2022) reached the same conclusion and added that both the cultivar and the drying history of the lot govern how much breakage occurs later during polishing. Chrastil and Zarins (1992) showed this change in the protein of stored rice, and Zhou et al. (2015) placed it at the centre of their explanation of rice ageing.

The three locations gave different values of head rice recovery, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 64.38% was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Purba Bardhaman came next with 64.08% and Nadia gave the lowest value of 62.87%. Each location took a letter group of its own. No location matched either of the others. The spread from best to poorest location came to 1.52 percentage points.

The three landraces also differed among themselves. The effect of variety was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 67.07%, followed by Radhunipagal with 62.26% and Gobindabhog with 62.00%. Each landrace fell into a letter group of its own. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 5.07 percentage points.

Storage changed head rice recovery. The difference was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 62.77% in fresh paddy, 64.06% at 4 months, 64.90% at 8 months and 63.37% at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 1.0%. The highest value came from 8 months and the lowest from fresh paddy.

The interaction of location with variety was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 68.88%. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 60.53%. The order of the landraces shifted from one location to another. At Nadia the sequence ran Kalojira, Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog. At Purba Bardhaman the sequence ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. At Birbhum/Howrah the sequence ran Kalojira, Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog. A shift of rank of this kind means the landraces answered the three environments differently.

The location by storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean was 65.64% for Birbhum/Howrah at 8 months. The lowest was 62.12% for Nadia at fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +0.4% at Nadia, +1.4% at Purba Bardhaman, +1.1% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations shifted by nearly equal amounts. Where the crop was grown made little difference to how storage acted.

The variety by storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean was 68.22% for Kalojira at 8 months. The lowest was 60.90% for Gobindabhog at fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change was +1.3% in Gobindabhog, +0.3% in Radhunipagal, +1.3% in Kalojira. The size of the change was similar in all three landraces. Storage acted on them equally.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 70.10% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months. The lowest value of 59.64% came from Gobindabhog grown at Nadia and sampled at 12 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Head rice recovery counts only the whole unbroken grains. Broken rice sells for far less than whole rice, so this is often the single most valuable milling figure. Li et al. (2018) reported the same balance, with milling quality governed more by the seed than by the field. The gap between landraces was much wider than the gap between locations, which agrees with Li et al. (2018), who found that milling quality is governed more by the genotype than by the growing environment. The reason is the same hardening described for milling percentage. The kernel therefore resists cracking better (Zhou et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2015). This shows that ageing helps only up to a point. A miller can therefore apply one ageing rule to all three landraces, but should still choose the landrace and the location together.

The three locations gave different values of the L/B ratio, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 1.865 was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 1.831 and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 1.607. All three locations were statistically distinct. All three differed among themselves. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.258.

The landraces likewise differed significantly. Variety had a highly significant effect. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value of 2.051, followed by Kalojira with 1.627 and Radhunipagal with 1.626. Kalojira and Radhunipagal carried a common letter. These two were on par with each other. Gobindabhog exceeded Radhunipagal by 0.426.

Storage changed the L/B ratio. The effect was significant at the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 1.789 in fresh paddy, 1.785 at 4 months, 1.753 at 8 months and 1.746 at 12 months. The value lost 2.4% over the year. Fresh paddy gave the highest value and 12 months the lowest.

Location and variety did not act independently, and their interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 2.113. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 1.170. Landrace ranking was not constant across the three districts. Nadia gave the order Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. Purba Bardhaman gave the order Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. Birbhum/Howrah gave the order Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. Such a change in order shows that the three environments did not affect every landrace alike.

The interaction of location with storage was highly significant. The highest mean was 1.882 for Nadia at 4 months. The lowest was 1.549 for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +1.6% at Nadia, -8.6% at Purba Bardhaman, -0.3% at Birbhum/Howrah. Grain from Purba Bardhaman changed the most and grain from Nadia the least. The spread was 10.2 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

The interaction of variety with storage was highly significant. The highest mean was 2.114 for Gobindabhog at 8 months. The lowest was 1.547 for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Over the twelve months the change was +0.3% in Gobindabhog, -7.4% in Radhunipagal, -0.3% in Kalojira. Radhunipagal moved the furthest and Gobindabhog the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The interaction of all three factors reached the 1% level. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 2.177 was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months. The lowest value of 0.991 came from Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months. The spread between these two cells was 1.186. No single factor alone produced a spread of this width. Location, landrace and storage acted in combination. Only the right combination of all three gives the best outcome.

The L/B ratio is grain length divided by grain breadth. It describes grain shape and it decides which market class a rice belongs to. Birbhum and Howrah produced the most slender grain at 1.865 and Purba Bardhaman the boldest at 1.607, with Nadia in between at 1.832. When filling is cut short by heat or by water stress, the grain does not reach its full length and the ratio falls. All three landraces sat well below the ratio of 2.5 to 3.0 that Kaul (1970) linked with long slender Basmati grain. This confirms that the aromatic rices of West Bengal belong to the small and medium grained group described by Singh et al. (2000). As the grain dries it shrinks more along its length than across its breadth, so the ratio falls. It shows up as significant only because the experimental error here was very low.

The three locations gave different values of moisture, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 13.34% was recorded at Nadia. Birbhum/Howrah came next with 13.28% and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 13.18%. No two locations shared a letter group. Every location stood apart from the other two. Between the top and bottom locations lay 0.16 percentage points.

The three landraces did not behave alike either. The varietal difference was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 13.78%, followed by Gobindabhog with 13.38% and Radhunipagal with 12.64%. The three landraces separated into distinct groups. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 1.14 percentage points.

Storage changed moisture. The effect reached the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 13.29% in fresh paddy, 12.74% at 4 months, 13.95% at 8 months and 13.10% at 12 months. A fall of 1.4% was recorded over the full year. The highest value came from 8 months and the lowest from 4 months.

The location by variety interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Nadia with 13.91%. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 12.58%. The same sequence of landraces appeared at all three sites. The order was Kalojira first, Gobindabhog second and Radhunipagal third. The interaction affected the size of the differences between landraces but left their direction intact.

The location by storage interaction reached the 1% level. The highest mean was 14.14% for Nadia at 8 months. The lowest was 12.68% for Nadia at 4 months. Over 12 months of storage the change came to -1.6% at Nadia, -1.1% at Purba Bardhaman and -1.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. The size of the change hardly differed between locations. Storage produced the same response in grain from all three locations.

The variety by storage interaction reached the 1% level. The highest mean was 14.45% for Kalojira at 8 months. The lowest was 12.21% for Radhunipagal at 4 months. The twelve-month change came to -2.1% in Gobindabhog, -0.9% in Radhunipagal and -1.1% in Kalojira. None of the three moved appreciably more than the others. There was no difference between them in response to storage.

Taken together the three factors interacted significantly. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 14.80% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months. The lowest value of 12.00% came from Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 4 months. The spread between these two cells was 2.80 percentage points. No single factor gives a spread as wide as this. The effect came from the three factors together. All three must be chosen well if the best result is wanted.

Moisture content decides whether stored paddy stays safe. Grain that is too wet attracts insects and moulds, while grain that is too dry shatters when handled. Since all lots were dried and stored together at Mohanpur, the closeness of the values confirms that the lots reached a similar equilibrium in the common storage environment, so the differences seen in the other traits are unlikely to be caused by one lot being kept wetter than another. Genkawa et al. (2008) showed that brown rice held in ordinary conditions keeps exchanging moisture with the surrounding air, so what matters is this running balance and not the moisture the grain started with. Müller et al. (2022) recommend holding stored grain between 11 and 15% moisture for this reason, and Duangkhamchan et al. (2024) showed in small farm barns in Thailand that moisture is rarely uniform through a stored lot, so parts of a heap can exceed the safe limit even when the average looks acceptable.

The three locations gave different values of the aroma score, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 2.232 was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 2.228 and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 2.127. Birbhum/Howrah and Nadia shared the same letter group. The difference between these two locations was too small to be real. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.104.

The three landraces also differed among themselves. The effect of variety was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 2.506, followed by Gobindabhog with 2.083 and Radhunipagal with 1.998. Each landrace fell into a letter group of its own. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 0.508.

Storage changed the aroma score. This effect was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 2.605 in fresh paddy, 2.326 at 4 months, 2.071 at 8 months and 1.780 at 12 months. By the end of the year the value had fallen 31.7%. The peak was in fresh paddy, the trough at 12 months.

Location and variety interacted significantly at the 1% level. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 2.561. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 1.962. Rank order of the landraces held at every location. Kalojira ranked first, Gobindabhog second and Radhunipagal third. Only the width of the varietal difference shifted; its direction was unaffected.

Location and storage period acted jointly. The highest mean was 2.646 for Nadia at fresh paddy. The lowest was 1.702 for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. Between harvest and 12 months, Nadia moved -31.1%, Purba Bardhaman -32.9% and Birbhum/Howrah -31.0%. The change was of similar magnitude at all three locations. Storage, which took place at a single site, affected grain from every location similarly.

Variety and storage period did not act independently. The highest mean was 2.908 for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 1.615 for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Over the year Gobindabhog moved -31.8%, Radhunipagal moved -32.8% and Kalojira moved -30.7%. Radhunipagal moved the furthest and Kalojira the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The L x V x S interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 2.953 was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 1.538 came from Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. The spread between these two cells was 1.415. The gap is much greater than that of any individual factor. All three factors operated jointly. The best outcome depends on getting each of the three right.

Aroma is the character that gives these landraces their premium value, and its loss removes the basis of that premium. Itani et al. (2004) put such location differences down to temperature during ripening, and later work has linked them to how much proline and related building blocks are available in the filling grain. Kim et al. (2023) reported the same pattern for overall sensory quality and found that it declined more gradually than germination rate, which suggests that grain can lose much of its eating quality before any outward sign of deterioration appears. The right storage period for aromatic rice is therefore a compromise between milling quality and eating quality. Jie et al. (2024) found that 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline in the aromatic cultivar Daohuaxiang fell by 43.9% within three months of conventional storage, against 25.7% under a 35% carbon dioxide atmosphere, and linked the loss to the rise in malondialdehyde and other markers of oxidative stress in the grain.

The three locations gave different values of total starch, and the effect of location was significant. The highest value of 72.97% was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 72.69% and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 72.35%. Birbhum/Howrah and Nadia shared the same letter group. The difference between these two locations was too small to be real. The best and poorest locations differed by 0.62 percentage points.

The three landraces also differed among themselves. The effect of variety was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 77.72%, followed by Gobindabhog with 72.19% and Radhunipagal with 68.10%. Each landrace fell into a letter group of its own. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 9.61 percentage points.

Storage changed total starch. The difference was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 73.36% in fresh paddy, 73.84% at 4 months, 71.81% at 8 months and 71.66% at 12 months. Across the twelve months the value dropped by 2.3%. The highest value came from 4 months and the lowest from 12 months.

The interaction of location with variety was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 78.07%. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Nadia with 67.37%. The three landraces kept the same order at each location. The sequence was Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal. The interaction altered how large the varietal differences were, not which way they ran.

The location and storage interaction was significant. The highest mean was 74.96% for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months. The lowest was 71.25% for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. By 12 months the three districts had changed -1.9%, -3.1% and -2.0% respectively. All three locations moved by close to the same amount. The effect of storage was the same whatever the district of origin.

Variety and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean was 79.07% for Kalojira at 4 months. The lowest was 66.95% for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Twelve months of storage gave -2.9% in Gobindabhog, -2.5% in Radhunipagal and -1.6% in Kalojira. The three landraces shifted by close to equal amounts. Storage affected all three similarly.

The three-way interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 81.12% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months. The lowest value of 65.71% came from Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months. The spread between these two cells was 15.41 percentage points. That range far exceeds the spread produced by any one factor alone. The three factors worked jointly. A good result therefore needs all three set correctly.

Starch is the main part of the rice grain and the main source of its food energy. Birbhum and Howrah gave the highest starch at 72.97%, Nadia 72.69% and Purba Bardhaman 72.35%, and Nadia was on par with both the others. The whole spread was only 0.62 percentage points. Starch is the bulk of the grain and its share does not vary much from field to field, so a narrow location effect is what one would expect. Zhou et al. (2015) put this process at the centre of their account of rice ageing. Zia-Ur-Rehman (2006) likewise found that how much starch is lost in stored cereals depends both on the grain and on the conditions of the store, and reported almost no loss when grain was kept at 10 °C.

The three locations gave different values of amylose, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 19.32% was recorded at Purba Bardhaman. Nadia came next with 18.77% and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 18.73%. Nadia and Birbhum/Howrah shared the same letter group. The difference between these two locations was too small to be real. A margin of 0.58 percentage points separated the best location from the worst.

The landraces likewise differed significantly. Variety had a highly significant effect. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 19.38%, followed by Radhunipagal with 18.87% and Gobindabhog with 18.58%. No two landraces shared a letter group. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 0.80 percentage points.

Storage changed amylose. The effect was significant at the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 17.77% in fresh paddy, 18.48% at 4 months, 19.46% at 8 months and 20.05% at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 12.8%. The highest value came from 12 months and the lowest from fresh paddy.

The location and variety interaction was not significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 19.74%. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 18.36%. Landrace order was unchanged from one location to the next. It went Kalojira, then Radhunipagal, then Gobindabhog. What the interaction changed was the magnitude of the varietal gap, not its sign.

Location and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean was 20.38% for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. The lowest was 17.42% for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +12.3% at Nadia, +11.6% at Purba Bardhaman, +14.6% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations shifted by nearly equal amounts. Where the crop was grown made little difference to how storage acted.

The interaction of variety with storage was non-significant. The highest mean was 20.39% for Kalojira at 12 months. The lowest was 17.38% for Gobindabhog at fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change was +13.5% in Gobindabhog, +13.5% in Radhunipagal, +11.5% in Kalojira. All three changed by similar amounts. The landraces responded to storage in the same way.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 20.68% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. The lowest value of 17.10% came from Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Amylose decides how cooked rice feels in the mouth. Rice low in amylose cooks moist and sticky, while rice with more amylose cooks drier and firmer (Mutters and Thompson, 2009). Purba Bardhaman gave the highest amylose at 19.31% and differed significantly from Nadia at 18.77% and Birbhum and Howrah at 18.73%, which were on par with each other. When freshly harvested, all three landraces fell in the low amylose class of 12 to 20% set out by Juliano (1992). The location effect was significant but small, and Li et al. (2018) also concluded that amylose is set more by the genotype than by the environment. Okpala et al. (2020) found that low temperature during grain filling raised both the amylose percentage and the elongation of cooked rice, which suggests that the location differences in amylose seen here arise partly from differences in ripening temperature among the districts.

The three locations gave different values of soluble protein, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 1.319% was recorded at Nadia. Birbhum/Howrah came next with 1.232% and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 1.154%. The three locations separated into distinct groups. The three locations all differed from one another. The spread from best to poorest location came to 0.165 percentage points.

The three landraces did not behave alike either. The varietal difference was highly significant. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value of 1.267%, followed by Radhunipagal with 1.219% and Kalojira with 1.218%. Radhunipagal and Kalojira carried a common letter. These two were on par with each other. Gobindabhog exceeded Kalojira by 0.049 percentage points.

Storage changed soluble protein. The effect reached the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 1.518% in fresh paddy, 1.368% at 4 months, 1.163% at 8 months and 0.890% at 12 months. The value lost 41.4% over the year. Fresh paddy stood highest; the 12-month sample stood lowest.

Location and variety did not act independently, and their interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 1.396%. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 1.084%. The landraces did not keep the same order at every location. The order at Nadia was Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. The order at Purba Bardhaman was Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. The order at Birbhum/Howrah was Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. Rank changing in this way indicates an uneven response to the growing environment.

The interaction of location with storage was non-significant. The highest mean was 1.584% for Nadia at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.802% for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. From fresh paddy to 12 months the value shifted -39.0% at Nadia, -44.9% at Purba Bardhaman and -40.5% at Birbhum/Howrah. The size of the change hardly differed between locations. Storage produced the same response in grain from all three locations.

No significant interaction appeared between variety and storage. The highest mean was 1.557% for Gobindabhog at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.863% for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Across twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -40.2%, Radhunipagal by -42.9% and Kalojira by -41.0%. The size of the change was similar in all three landraces. Storage acted on them equally.

The interaction of all three factors reached the 1% level. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.707% was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 0.781% came from Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. The spread between these two cells was 0.926 percentage points. No single factor alone produced a spread of this width. Location, landrace and storage acted in combination. Only the right combination of all three gives the best outcome.

Soluble protein is the part of the grain protein that can be pulled out into solution. The location effect itself is likely to come from differences in soil nitrogen and in temperature while the grain was filling. Li et al. (2018) found that environment mattered more than genotype for protein content, and reported that warmer weather during ripening pushed grain protein up. The reason is well known. Chrastil and Zarins (1992) showed that storage builds sulphur bridges within the main rice protein and pushes the smaller pieces into larger clumps. Those clumps do not dissolve as readily, so the test records less protein even though the nitrogen in the grain has hardly changed. This distinction matters when the result is read. So the nutritional value does fall, even if the total protein stays put.

The three locations gave different values of fat, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 1.207% was recorded at Nadia. Purba Bardhaman came next with 1.149% and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 1.144%. Purba Bardhaman and Birbhum/Howrah shared the same letter group. The difference between these two locations was too small to be real. Between the top and bottom locations lay 0.063 percentage points.

The three landraces also differed among themselves. The effect of variety was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 1.256%, followed by Gobindabhog with 1.215% and Radhunipagal with 1.028%. Each landrace fell into a letter group of its own. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 0.228 percentage points.

Storage changed fat. This effect was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 1.382% in fresh paddy, 1.239% at 4 months, 1.095% at 8 months and 0.950% at 12 months. A fall of 31.3% was recorded over the full year. The maximum fell on fresh paddy and the minimum on 12 months.

The location by variety interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Nadia with 1.313%. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.953%. The same sequence of landraces appeared at all three sites. The order was Kalojira first, Gobindabhog second and Radhunipagal third. The interaction affected the size of the differences between landraces but left their direction intact.

No significant interaction arose between location and storage. The highest mean was 1.421% for Nadia at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.931% for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months. Over 12 months of storage the change came to -31.2% at Nadia, -30.8% at Purba Bardhaman and -31.8% at Birbhum/Howrah. The change was of similar magnitude at all three locations. Storage, which took place at a single site, affected grain from every location similarly.

Variety and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 1.491% for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.832% for Radhunipagal at 12 months. The twelve-month change came to -31.5% in Gobindabhog, -31.0% in Radhunipagal and -31.2% in Kalojira. None of the three moved appreciably more than the others. There was no difference between them in response to storage.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.558% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 0.743% came from Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 12 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Rice contains only a little fat, but that fat has an influence on flavour and on storage life out of all proportion to how little of it there is. Most of the fat in rice sits in the bran and the embryo, so the location effect here reflects differences in how thick those layers were and in how much was left behind after polishing. Genkawa et al. (2008) noted that fat acidity climbs quickly in stored rice and is widely used for this reason as a measure of how far grain has deteriorated. Kim et al. (2023) confirmed in a recent study of post-harvest handling that fat acidity and sensory quality both worsen steadily as storage temperature and storage period increase. The small compounds produced when rice fat oxidises are what give old rice its stale smell, and they work against whatever aroma is left in the grain. Zhou et al. (2002) described the same link between fat breakdown and flavour change in stored rice.

The three locations gave different values of ash, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 0.828% was recorded at Nadia. Birbhum/Howrah came next with 0.824% and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 0.697%. Each location took a letter group of its own. No location matched either of the others. The best and poorest locations differed by 0.131 percentage points.

The three landraces did not behave alike either. The varietal difference was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 0.989%, followed by Radhunipagal with 0.767% and Gobindabhog with 0.593%. The three landraces separated into distinct groups. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 0.396 percentage points.

Storage changed ash. The difference was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 0.800% in fresh paddy, 0.780% at 4 months, 0.772% at 8 months and 0.779% at 12 months. By the end of the year the value had fallen 2.7%. Fresh paddy gave the highest value and 8 months the lowest.

Location and variety interacted significantly at the 1% level. The best combination was Radhunipagal at Nadia with 1.161%. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 0.368%. Rank order changed with the location. At Nadia the ranking ran Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. At Purba Bardhaman the ranking ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. At Birbhum/Howrah the ranking ran Kalojira, Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog. This reordering shows that the landraces reacted to their surroundings in different degrees.

Location and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 0.866% for Nadia at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.672% for Purba Bardhaman at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was -7.0% at Nadia, -1.6% at Purba Bardhaman, +0.8% at Birbhum/Howrah. Grain from Nadia changed the most and grain from Birbhum/Howrah the least. The spread was 7.8 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

The interaction of variety with storage was highly significant. The highest mean was 0.991% for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.581% for Gobindabhog at 8 months. Over the year Gobindabhog moved -4.4%, Radhunipagal moved -3.8% and Kalojira moved -0.8%. Gobindabhog moved the furthest and Kalojira the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

Taken together the three factors interacted significantly. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.249% was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 0.350% came from Gobindabhog grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The spread between these two cells was 0.899 percentage points. That range is far wider than any one factor produces alone. The effect came from the three factors together. All three must be chosen well if the best result is wanted.

Ash is what is left after the grain is burnt off, and it stands for the total mineral content. Verma and Srivastav (2017) also found large differences in ash among Indian aromatic rices and reported aromatic types to be better than non-aromatic ones on this count. Patra et al. (2024) likewise recorded higher ash in Tulaipanji grain from West Bengal when the crop was raised on organic nutrient sources, which shows that ash responds to soil supply as well as to the landrace. Ash should not really change during storage, because minerals are neither made nor lost from grain sitting in a store. It shows up as significant only because the coefficient of variation for this trait was 0.23%, which is unusually low. The most likely explanation is that ash was worked out on a fresh weight basis, so it shifts slightly as the moisture in the grain moves up and down.

The three locations gave different values of total phenol, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 0.8232 mg GAE/g was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 0.7145 mg GAE/g and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 0.4614 mg GAE/g. All three locations were statistically distinct. All three differed among themselves. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.3617 mg GAE/g.

The three landraces did not behave alike either. The varietal difference was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 0.7812 mg GAE/g, followed by Radhunipagal with 0.6459 mg GAE/g and Gobindabhog with 0.5719 mg GAE/g. The three landraces separated into distinct groups. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 0.2093 mg GAE/g.

Storage changed total phenol. The effect was significant at the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 0.8868 mg GAE/g in fresh paddy, 0.7590 mg GAE/g at 4 months, 0.5976 mg GAE/g at 8 months and 0.4220 mg GAE/g at 12 months. Across the twelve months the value dropped by 52.4%. The peak was in fresh paddy, the trough at 12 months.

The interaction of location with variety was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.9337 mg GAE/g. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.3891 mg GAE/g. Rank order of the landraces held at every location. Kalojira ranked first, Radhunipagal second and Gobindabhog third. Only the width of the varietal difference shifted; its direction was unaffected.

The interaction of location with storage was highly significant. The highest mean was 1.0966 mg GAE/g for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.3237 mg GAE/g for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. Between harvest and 12 months, Nadia moved -54.9%, Purba Bardhaman -46.4% and Birbhum/Howrah -53.6%. Grain from Nadia changed the most and grain from Purba Bardhaman the least. The spread was 8.5 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

The variety by storage interaction reached the 1% level. The highest mean was 1.0325 mg GAE/g for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.3620 mg GAE/g for Gobindabhog at 12 months. Twelve months of storage gave -53.0% in Gobindabhog, -53.1% in Radhunipagal and -51.4% in Kalojira. The three landraces shifted by close to equal amounts. Storage affected all three similarly.

The L x V x S interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.2632 mg GAE/g was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 0.2734 mg GAE/g came from Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. The spread between these two cells was 0.9898 mg GAE/g. The gap is much greater than that of any individual factor. All three factors operated jointly. The best outcome depends on getting each of the three right.

Phenolic compounds are the main health promoting substances in rice. They scavenge free radicals in the body and are a large part of why pigmented rices are valued. The difference between locations was unusually large. Birbhum and Howrah gave nearly twice the phenol content of Purba Bardhaman. A gap of that size shows that growing conditions have a powerful say in how much phenolic material the grain builds up. Zhang et al. (2010) showed that black rice bran carries far more phenolic material than unpigmented rice. Shao et al. (2014) measured how these compounds are spread between the bran, the embryo and the endosperm of white, red and black rice. Ordinary storage in West Bengal is nearer the warmer of those two figures, which helps explain how severe the loss was.

The three locations gave different values of total flavonoid, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 19.09 mg QE/100 g was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 16.74 mg QE/100 g and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 12.07 mg QE/100 g. No two locations shared a letter group. Every location stood apart from the other two. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 7.02 mg QE/100 g.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 18.06 mg QE/100 g, followed by Radhunipagal with 15.86 mg QE/100 g and Gobindabhog with 13.98 mg QE/100 g. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 4.08 mg QE/100 g.

Storage changed total flavonoid. The effect reached the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 19.57 mg QE/100 g in fresh paddy, 17.14 mg QE/100 g at 4 months, 14.87 mg QE/100 g at 8 months and 12.28 mg QE/100 g at 12 months. The value lost 37.3% over the year. Fresh paddy stood highest; the 12-month sample stood lowest.

The location and variety interaction was not significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 21.19 mg QE/100 g. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 10.32 mg QE/100 g. The three landraces kept the same order at each location. The sequence was Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog. The interaction altered how large the varietal differences were, not which way they ran.

The location by storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean was 22.87 mg QE/100 g for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. The lowest was 8.41 mg QE/100 g for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. By 12 months the three districts had changed -35.1%, -46.2% and -33.1% respectively. All three locations moved by close to the same amount. The effect of storage was the same whatever the district of origin.

The variety by storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean was 21.80 mg QE/100 g for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 10.38 mg QE/100 g for Gobindabhog at 12 months. Across twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -40.6%, Radhunipagal by -36.2% and Kalojira by -35.5%. All three changed by similar amounts. The landraces responded to storage in the same way.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 25.16 mg QE/100 g was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 6.52 mg QE/100 g came from Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Flavonoids are one family within the larger group of phenolic compounds and they carry much of the antioxidant activity of pigmented grain. Plants build up flavonoids partly in response to stress from strong sunlight, drought or poor soil, so a harsher growing environment often yields grain richer in these compounds even when it yields less of it. The likely reason is that many flavonoids in grain carry attached sugar molecules, which makes them steadier against oxidation than simple phenolic acids. Kunnam et al. (2023) found the environment to be the main source of variation in the phenolic fraction of rice across locations, and Naveed et al. (2023) recorded a loss of antioxidant constituents of up to 50% over six months of storage; the flavonoid data here follow both patterns.

The three locations gave different values of antioxidant capacity, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 41.35 mg TE/100 g was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 34.83 mg TE/100 g and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 28.73 mg TE/100 g. The three locations separated into distinct groups. The three locations all differed from one another. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 12.62 mg TE/100 g.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 40.26 mg TE/100 g, followed by Radhunipagal with 34.74 mg TE/100 g and Gobindabhog with 29.91 mg TE/100 g. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 10.34 mg TE/100 g.

Storage changed antioxidant capacity. This effect was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 53.44 mg TE/100 g in fresh paddy, 38.95 mg TE/100 g at 4 months, 27.57 mg TE/100 g at 8 months and 19.92 mg TE/100 g at 12 months. A fall of 62.7% was recorded over the full year. The maximum fell on fresh paddy and the minimum on 12 months.

Location and variety did not act independently, and their interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 45.63 mg TE/100 g. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 24.69 mg TE/100 g. Landrace order was unchanged from one location to the next. It went Kalojira, then Radhunipagal, then Gobindabhog. What the interaction changed was the magnitude of the varietal gap, not its sign.

The location by storage interaction reached the 1% level. The highest mean was 62.11 mg TE/100 g for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. The lowest was 13.57 mg TE/100 g for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. From fresh paddy to 12 months the value shifted -61.2% at Nadia, -70.4% at Purba Bardhaman and -58.3% at Birbhum/Howrah. Grain from Purba Bardhaman changed the most and grain from Birbhum/Howrah the least. The spread was 12.1 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

Variety and storage period did not act independently. The highest mean was 61.13 mg TE/100 g for Kalojira at fresh paddy. The lowest was 16.26 mg TE/100 g for Gobindabhog at 12 months. The twelve-month change came to -63.8% in Gobindabhog, -64.6% in Radhunipagal and -60.2% in Kalojira. Radhunipagal moved the furthest and Kalojira the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The three-way interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 69.63 mg TE/100 g was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 10.42 mg TE/100 g came from Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. The spread between these two cells was 59.21 mg TE/100 g. That range far exceeds the spread produced by any one factor alone. The three factors worked jointly. A good result therefore needs all three set correctly.

Antioxidant capacity measures how well an extract of the grain can neutralise free radicals. Grain from Birbhum and Howrah is therefore the pick of the three locations for anyone valuing aromatic rice for its health giving properties. If phenolics alone were responsible, antioxidant capacity could not have dropped faster than they did. Because Birbhum and Howrah also started highest, the gap between the locations widened over the year rather than closing. Naveed et al. (2023) stored five brown Basmati varieties for three and six months at 5 and 25 °C and found that antioxidant activity fell by up to 50%, the loss growing with both time and temperature, while oleic and linoleic acids were also depleted. On the location side, Kunnam et al. (2023) evaluated six rice genotypes at three sites in Thailand and found the environment to be the main source of variation in total phenolic content and antioxidant capacity, although some genotypes held their values steadily across sites.

The three locations gave different values of phytic acid, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 339.23 mg/100 g was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Purba Bardhaman came next with 283.61 mg/100 g and Nadia gave the lowest value of 216.14 mg/100 g. Each location took a letter group of its own. No location matched either of the others. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 123.09 mg/100 g.

The three landraces did not behave alike either. The varietal difference was highly significant. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value of 336.04 mg/100 g, followed by Radhunipagal with 306.86 mg/100 g and Kalojira with 196.07 mg/100 g. The three landraces separated into distinct groups. Gobindabhog exceeded Kalojira by 139.97 mg/100 g.

Storage changed phytic acid. The difference was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 350.10 mg/100 g in fresh paddy, 309.79 mg/100 g at 4 months, 248.66 mg/100 g at 8 months and 210.08 mg/100 g at 12 months. By the end of the year the value had fallen 40.0%. Fresh paddy gave the highest value and 12 months the lowest.

The location by variety interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 460.67 mg/100 g. The poorest was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 175.02 mg/100 g. The order of the landraces shifted from one location to another. At Nadia the sequence ran Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. At Purba Bardhaman the sequence ran Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog and Kalojira. At Birbhum/Howrah the sequence ran Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. A shift of rank of this kind means the landraces answered the three environments differently.

Location and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean was 409.95 mg/100 g for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. The lowest was 144.22 mg/100 g for Nadia at 12 months. Over 12 months of storage the change came to -49.9% at Nadia, -36.8% at Purba Bardhaman and -35.8% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations shifted by nearly equal amounts. Where the crop was grown made little difference to how storage acted.

Variety and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 408.86 mg/100 g for Gobindabhog at fresh paddy. The lowest was 139.17 mg/100 g for Kalojira at 12 months. Over the year Gobindabhog moved -35.5%, Radhunipagal moved -41.3% and Kalojira moved -45.2%. Kalojira moved the furthest and Gobindabhog the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The interaction of all three factors reached the 1% level. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 513.34 mg/100 g was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 131.60 mg/100 g came from Gobindabhog grown at Nadia and sampled at 12 months. The spread between these two cells was 381.74 mg/100 g. No single factor alone produced a spread of this width. Location, landrace and storage acted in combination. Only the right combination of all three gives the best outcome.

Phytic acid is an anti-nutrient. It locks up iron and zinc so the human gut cannot absorb them, which matters a great deal in a country where rice is the main food and iron and zinc shortages are common. From a nutritional point of view the low figure at Nadia is the desirable one, because less phytic acid means the iron and zinc in the grain are easier for the body to absorb. Gobindabhog held far more phytic acid than Kalojira, and the same order held at all three locations, so the difference is genetic. A breeder can therefore select for lower phytate without using induced mutants. No earlier study of this character in these landraces, or of its change during storage, was found among the literature reviewed in Chapter II, so the present figures stand as a first record for the cultivars concerned.

The three locations gave different values of the L* value, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 76.59 was recorded at Purba Bardhaman. Nadia came next with 74.77 and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 74.23. All three locations were statistically distinct. All three differed among themselves. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 2.36.

The landraces likewise differed significantly. Variety had a highly significant effect. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value of 75.74, followed by Gobindabhog with 75.40 and Kalojira with 74.44. No two landraces shared a letter group. Radhunipagal exceeded Kalojira by 1.30.

Storage changed the L* value. The effect was significant at the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 75.02 in fresh paddy, 75.38 at 4 months, 75.00 at 8 months and 75.39 at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 0.5%. The highest value came from 12 months and the lowest from 8 months.

Location and variety interacted significantly at the 1% level. The best combination was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 77.51. The poorest was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 72.23. Landrace ranking was not constant across the three districts. Nadia gave the order Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. Purba Bardhaman gave the order Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. Birbhum/Howrah gave the order Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. Such a change in order shows that the three environments did not affect every landrace alike.

Location and storage period acted jointly. The highest mean was 76.85 for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. The lowest was 73.84 for Birbhum/Howrah at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +1.4% at Nadia, +0.1% at Purba Bardhaman, -0.0% at Birbhum/Howrah. The size of the change hardly differed between locations. Storage produced the same response in grain from all three locations.

The interaction of variety with storage was highly significant. The highest mean was 75.83 for Radhunipagal at 8 months. The lowest was 74.05 for Kalojira at fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change was +0.2% in Gobindabhog, +0.2% in Radhunipagal, +1.1% in Kalojira. The size of the change was similar in all three landraces. Storage acted on them equally.

Taken together the three factors interacted significantly. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 79.71 was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 71.80 came from Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 4 months. The spread between these two cells was 7.91. The spread far exceeds what any factor gives alone. The effect came from the three factors together. All three must be chosen well if the best result is wanted.

The L* value measures how bright the milled rice looks. Surface brightness after polishing depends on how smooth and how translucent the kernel is, and both are set while the grain is filling. A high L* is therefore not always a sign of better quality. The brightness recorded there may therefore reflect a chalkier endosperm rather than better polishing. The same landrace also gave the highest phenol, flavonoid and antioxidant readings in this study, which fits, because those pigments are themselves phenolic compounds. Zhang et al. (2010) described the same pigment load in the bran of black rice. Yanxia et al. (2018) reached the same conclusion for milled rice kept at room temperature, reporting only a small change in L*. Colour is therefore not the attribute that limits how long these landraces can be kept.

The three locations gave different values of the a* value, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of -1.154 was recorded at Nadia. Birbhum/Howrah came next with -1.222 and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of -2.208. Nadia and Birbhum/Howrah shared the same letter group. The difference between these two locations was too small to be real. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 1.054.

The three landraces did not behave alike either. The varietal difference was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of -0.702, followed by Radhunipagal with -1.630 and Gobindabhog with -2.252. The three landraces separated into distinct groups. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 1.550.

Storage changed the a* value. The effect reached the 1% level. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were -3.310 in fresh paddy, -0.764 at 4 months, -1.176 at 8 months and -0.862 at 12 months. Across the twelve months the value dropped by 74.0%. The highest value came from 4 months and the lowest from fresh paddy.

The interaction of location with variety was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 1.325. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with -4.563. The landraces did not keep the same order at every location. The order at Nadia was Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. The order at Purba Bardhaman was Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. The order at Birbhum/Howrah was Kalojira, Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog. Rank changing in this way indicates an uneven response to the growing environment.

Location and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 0.138 for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months. The lowest was -4.548 for Purba Bardhaman at fresh paddy. Between harvest and 12 months, Nadia moved -0.6%, Purba Bardhaman -72.6% and Birbhum/Howrah -95.2%. Grain from Birbhum/Howrah changed the most and grain from Nadia the least. The spread was 94.6 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

The variety by storage interaction reached the 1% level. The highest mean was -0.499 for Kalojira at 12 months. The lowest was -4.885 for Gobindabhog at fresh paddy. Twelve months of storage gave -76.3% in Gobindabhog, -79.0% in Radhunipagal and -18.5% in Kalojira. Radhunipagal moved the furthest and Kalojira the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The L x V x S interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.790 was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 12 months. The lowest value of -13.290 came from Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. The spread between these two cells was 15.080. The gap is much greater than that of any individual factor. All three factors operated jointly. The best outcome depends on getting each of the three right.

The a* value shows where a sample sits between green and red. This fits with the brighter, chalkier grain recorded at Purba Bardhaman, since grain that has not filled completely tends to hold more of its immature pigment. Kalojira therefore sat closest to neutral even in fresh grain. The same pigments explain why Kalojira ranked highest for phenol, flavonoid and antioxidant capacity in this study. It explains the greenish cast that freshly milled rice often shows and that disappears after the first storage season. Those same reactions explain why the extractable phenol content fell so steeply in this study, and Zhou et al. (2004) reported a similar loss of phenolic acids in stored rice. The reason is that Kalojira started much closer to neutral, so it had less green pigment to lose. Because the grand mean is negative, the coefficient of variation also prints as a negative figure, and it should be read as 14.19%.

The three locations gave different values of the b* value, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 113.67 was recorded at Purba Bardhaman. Nadia came next with 113.14 and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 111.35. No two locations shared a letter group. Every location stood apart from the other two. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 2.32.

The three landraces also differed among themselves. The effect of variety was highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 113.16, followed by Radhunipagal with 112.64 and Gobindabhog with 112.35. Each landrace fell into a letter group of its own. Kalojira exceeded Gobindabhog by 0.81.

Storage changed the b* value. This effect was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 108.35 in fresh paddy, 114.51 at 4 months, 113.94 at 8 months and 114.07 at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 5.3%. The highest value came from 4 months and the lowest from fresh paddy.

Location and variety did not act independently, and their interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 115.48. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 109.26. Rank order changed with the location. At Nadia the ranking ran Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. At Purba Bardhaman the ranking ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. At Birbhum/Howrah the ranking ran Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. This reordering shows that the landraces reacted to their surroundings in different degrees.

The interaction of location with storage was highly significant. The highest mean was 115.85 for Purba Bardhaman at 4 months. The lowest was 105.12 for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +1.2% at Nadia, +7.2% at Purba Bardhaman, +7.7% at Birbhum/Howrah. Grain from Nadia changed the most and grain from Birbhum/Howrah the least. The spread was 6.5 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

Variety and storage period did not act independently. The highest mean was 115.00 for Radhunipagal at 4 months. The lowest was 106.10 for Gobindabhog at fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change was +7.8% in Gobindabhog, +7.4% in Radhunipagal, +0.9% in Kalojira. Kalojira moved the furthest and Gobindabhog the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The three-way interaction was highly significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 117.48 was recorded by Kalojira grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 4 months. The lowest value of 92.38 came from Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at fresh paddy. The spread between these two cells was 25.10. That range far exceeds the spread produced by any one factor alone. The three factors worked jointly. A good result therefore needs all three set correctly.

The b* value shows where a sample sits between blue and yellow. This is expected, because polishing removes most of the coloured bran and what is left behind differs little between these three landraces. Once curing was over, b* stopped moving, which agrees with Yanxia et al. (2018), who found no significant change in the b* value of milled rice during ordinary storage. This steadiness matters, because yellowing is usually taken as a sign that grain is going bad. Genkawa et al. (2008) linked yellowing to high moisture and high temperature rather than to the passage of time alone, and Wang et al. (2025) similarly found that the yellowing rate of newly harvested rice depended on how the grain was dried rather than on how long it was subsequently held.

The three locations gave different values of the total colour difference, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 42.29 was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Purba Bardhaman came next with 41.87 and Nadia gave the lowest value of 39.69. The three locations separated into distinct groups. The three locations all differed from one another. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 2.60.

The landraces likewise differed significantly. Variety had a highly significant effect. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value of 41.42, followed by Gobindabhog with 41.31 and Kalojira with 41.12. Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog carried a common letter. These two were on par with each other. Radhunipagal exceeded Kalojira by 0.30.

Storage changed the total colour difference. The difference was highly significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 27.22 in fresh paddy, 46.08 at 4 months, 45.71 at 8 months and 46.12 at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 69.4%. The highest value came from 12 months and the lowest from fresh paddy.

The location by variety interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 45.56. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Nadia with 38.76. The order of the landraces shifted from one location to another. At Nadia the sequence ran Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. At Purba Bardhaman the sequence ran Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog and Kalojira. At Birbhum/Howrah the sequence ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. A shift of rank of this kind means the landraces answered the three environments differently.

The location by storage interaction reached the 1% level. The highest mean was 47.55 for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. The lowest was 22.41 for Nadia at fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +103.8% at Nadia, +86.4% at Purba Bardhaman, +33.7% at Birbhum/Howrah. Grain from Birbhum/Howrah changed the most and grain from Nadia the least. The spread was 70.1 percentage points. The rate of change during storage was therefore not the same for grain from all three locations.

Variety and storage interacted significantly at the 1% level. The highest mean was 46.81 for Radhunipagal at 4 months. The lowest was 26.08 for Radhunipagal at fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change was +71.2% in Gobindabhog, +77.2% in Radhunipagal, +60.7% in Kalojira. Kalojira moved the furthest and Radhunipagal the least. The three landraces did not lose or gain at the same rate during storage.

The interaction of all three factors reached the 1% level. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 49.74 was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months. The lowest value of 18.82 came from Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The spread between these two cells was 30.92. No single factor alone produced a spread of this width. Location, landrace and storage acted in combination. Only the right combination of all three gives the best outcome.

The total colour difference brings L*, a* and b* together into one number. It is a convenient single figure for judging how far a sample sits from a reference colour. Birbhum and Howrah gave the largest colour difference at 42.29, with Purba Bardhaman at 41.87 and Nadia lowest at 39.69. This index combines all three colour readings. Its behaviour therefore follows from theirs. For the trade this means that stored aromatic rice is unlikely to be turned down on colour within a year, so long as the moisture is kept in check. No earlier study of this character in these landraces, or of its change during storage, was found among the literature reviewed in Chapter II, so the present figures stand as a first record for the cultivars concerned.

The three locations gave different values of copper, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 0.051 ppm was recorded at Nadia. Purba Bardhaman came next with 0.035 ppm and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 0.025 ppm. Each location took a letter group of its own. No location matched either of the others. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.026 ppm.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value of 0.039 ppm, followed by Gobindabhog with 0.038 ppm and Radhunipagal with 0.034 ppm. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Kalojira exceeded Radhunipagal by 0.004 ppm.

Storage changed copper. The effect was not significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 0.037 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.037 ppm at 4 months, 0.037 ppm at 8 months and 0.037 ppm at 12 months. The value lost 0.7% over the year. The peak was in fresh paddy, the trough at 4 months.

Location and variety interacted significantly at the 1% level. The best combination was Radhunipagal at Nadia with 0.059 ppm. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.018 ppm. Landrace ranking was not constant across the three districts. Nadia gave the order Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog and Kalojira. Purba Bardhaman gave the order Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. Birbhum/Howrah gave the order Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. Such a change in order shows that the three environments did not affect every landrace alike.

The interaction of location with storage was non-significant. The highest mean was 0.052 ppm for Nadia at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.024 ppm for Birbhum/Howrah at fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was -3.3% at Nadia, -0.4% at Purba Bardhaman, +4.5% at Birbhum/Howrah. The change was of similar magnitude at all three locations. Storage, which took place at a single site, affected grain from every location similarly.

Variety and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean was 0.040 ppm for Kalojira at 8 months. The lowest was 0.033 ppm for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Across twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -0.6%, Radhunipagal by -0.3% and Kalojira by -1.2%. None of the three moved appreciably more than the others. There was no difference between them in response to storage.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 0.060 ppm was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months. The lowest value of 0.018 ppm came from Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Copper is needed in small quantities in the human diet, and rice supplies part of it. Grain mineral content is settled during the growing season, when the roots take the element up and the plant moves it into the developing grain. So this difference comes from the copper status of the three soils and from the chemical conditions that decide how much of it the plant can reach. The spread of 0.005 ppm is very narrow, so the landrace has far less say over copper than the soil does. Reports on these minerals in the aromatic landraces of West Bengal are few. Singh et al. (2022) found wide cultivar differences in mineral content among the pigmented rices of north-east India, and Naveed et al. (2023) recorded that the ash and mineral contents of brown Basmati stayed steady through six months of storage while the antioxidant fraction fell, which agrees with the stability of the minerals seen here.

The three locations gave different values of iron, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 0.481 ppm was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Nadia came next with 0.227 ppm and Purba Bardhaman gave the lowest value of 0.171 ppm. All three locations were statistically distinct. All three differed among themselves. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.309 ppm.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value of 0.525 ppm, followed by Radhunipagal with 0.224 ppm and Kalojira with 0.130 ppm. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Gobindabhog exceeded Kalojira by 0.395 ppm.

Storage changed iron. The effect was not significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 0.293 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.293 ppm at 4 months, 0.294 ppm at 8 months and 0.292 ppm at 12 months. A fall of 0.5% was recorded over the full year. The highest value came from 8 months and the lowest from 12 months.

The interaction of location with variety was highly significant. The best combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 1.338 ppm. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.049 ppm. The landraces did not keep the same order at every location. The order at Nadia was Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. The order at Purba Bardhaman was Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog and Kalojira. The order at Birbhum/Howrah was Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal. Rank changing in this way indicates an uneven response to the growing environment.

No significant interaction arose between location and storage. The highest mean was 0.482 ppm for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months. The lowest was 0.169 ppm for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was -1.2% at Nadia, -1.8% at Purba Bardhaman, +0.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. All three locations moved by close to the same amount. The effect of storage was the same whatever the district of origin.

The interaction of variety with storage was non-significant. The highest mean was 0.527 ppm for Gobindabhog at 8 months. The lowest was 0.126 ppm for Kalojira at 12 months. Over the twelve months the change was +0.0% in Gobindabhog, +0.8% in Radhunipagal, -4.6% in Kalojira. The three landraces shifted by close to equal amounts. Storage affected all three similarly.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.341 ppm was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 4 months. The lowest value of 0.048 ppm came from Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Iron shortage is one of the most widespread nutritional problems in India, and rice is a poor source of it, so any natural variation among rice types is worth knowing about. The higher iron at Birbhum and Howrah fits the soils of those districts. Aged grain therefore delivers more usable iron than fresh grain, even though the total is unchanged.
