The same landrace therefore gave both a very high and a very low result depending on the location, which is a strong warning against judging iron content from one location. Singh et al. (2022) analysed eleven black, red and white rice cultivars of north-east India and recorded wide ranges in iron, zinc and other minerals alongside phenolic content, with the pigmented types generally the richer.

The three locations gave different values of zinc, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 0.748 ppm was recorded at Nadia. Purba Bardhaman came next with 0.438 ppm and Birbhum/Howrah gave the lowest value of 0.397 ppm. No two locations shared a letter group. Every location stood apart from the other two. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.351 ppm.

Differences among the landraces were equally clear. Landrace differences reached the 1% level. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value of 0.708 ppm, followed by Kalojira with 0.486 ppm and Gobindabhog with 0.388 ppm. All three landraces were statistically distinct. Radhunipagal exceeded Gobindabhog by 0.320 ppm.

Storage changed zinc. The effect was not significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 0.530 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.528 ppm at 4 months, 0.528 ppm at 8 months and 0.524 ppm at 12 months. By the end of the year the value had fallen 1.1%. Fresh paddy stood highest; the 12-month sample stood lowest.

Location and variety did not act independently, and their interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Radhunipagal at Nadia with 1.375 ppm. The poorest was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.343 ppm. Rank order changed with the location. At Nadia the ranking ran Radhunipagal, Kalojira and Gobindabhog. At Purba Bardhaman the ranking ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. At Birbhum/Howrah the ranking ran Kalojira, Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog. This reordering shows that the landraces reacted to their surroundings in different degrees.

The location by storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean was 0.753 ppm for Nadia at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.395 ppm for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months. By 12 months the three districts had changed -1.9%, -0.4% and -0.6% respectively. The three locations shifted by nearly equal amounts. Where the crop was grown made little difference to how storage acted.

No significant interaction appeared between variety and storage. The highest mean was 0.712 ppm for Radhunipagal at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.383 ppm for Gobindabhog at 12 months. The twelve-month change came to -2.0% in Gobindabhog, -0.5% in Radhunipagal and -1.3% in Kalojira. All three changed by similar amounts. The landraces responded to storage in the same way.

The three factor interaction was significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 1.382 ppm was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at fresh paddy. The lowest value of 0.333 ppm came from Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 12 months. The spread between these two cells was 1.049 ppm. A gap of this width comes only from the factors acting together. The effect came from the three factors together. All three must be chosen well if the best result is wanted.

Zinc, like iron, is often short in diets built around rice, and again the grain is a modest source. So the two minerals are taken up and stored by at least partly different routes inside the plant, and none of the three landraces is good for both. Zinc absorption is strongly blocked by phytate, so the improving ratio between them over twelve months represents a genuine if modest nutritional gain that partly offsets the losses seen in other traits. Reports on these minerals in the aromatic landraces of West Bengal are few. Singh et al. (2022) found wide cultivar differences in mineral content among the pigmented rices of north-east India, and Naveed et al. (2023) recorded that the ash and mineral contents of brown Basmati stayed steady through six months of storage while the antioxidant fraction fell, which agrees with the stability of the minerals seen here.

The three locations gave different values of manganese, and the effect of location was highly significant. The highest value of 0.133 ppm was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah. Purba Bardhaman came next with 0.132 ppm and Nadia gave the lowest value of 0.093 ppm. Birbhum/Howrah and Purba Bardhaman shared the same letter group. The difference between these two locations was too small to be real. The gap between the best and the poorest location was 0.040 ppm.

The three landraces also differed among themselves. The effect of variety was highly significant. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value of 0.120 ppm, followed by Gobindabhog with 0.120 ppm and Kalojira with 0.117 ppm. Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog carried a common letter. These two were on par with each other. Radhunipagal exceeded Kalojira by 0.003 ppm.

Storage changed manganese. The effect was not significant. Taken in order of sampling date, the values were 0.119 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.119 ppm at 4 months, 0.119 ppm at 8 months and 0.120 ppm at 12 months. Over the full year the value increased by 0.5%. The highest value came from 12 months and the lowest from 4 months.

The location by variety interaction was highly significant. The best combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.143 ppm. The poorest was Radhunipagal at Nadia with 0.088 ppm. The order of the landraces shifted from one location to another. At Nadia the sequence ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal. At Purba Bardhaman the sequence ran Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. At Birbhum/Howrah the sequence ran Kalojira, Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog. A shift of rank of this kind means the landraces answered the three environments differently.

Location and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean was 0.133 ppm for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months. The lowest was 0.092 ppm for Nadia at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change was +0.4% at Nadia, +0.8% at Purba Bardhaman, +0.3% at Birbhum/Howrah. The size of the change hardly differed between locations. Storage produced the same response in grain from all three locations.

The variety by storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean was 0.121 ppm for Radhunipagal at fresh paddy. The lowest was 0.117 ppm for Kalojira at 8 months. Over the twelve months the change was +0.7% in Gobindabhog, -0.4% in Radhunipagal, +1.2% in Kalojira. The size of the change was similar in all three landraces. Storage acted on them equally.

The three factor interaction was not significant. Out of the thirty six treatment combinations the highest value of 0.146 ppm was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months. The lowest value of 0.087 ppm came from Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months. This interaction was not significant. These two extreme cells should not be read as real differences alone. The main effects give the safer picture.

Manganese is a trace element needed in small quantities, and rice grain supplies a useful share of it. In flooded rice soils the availability of manganese depends heavily on how reduced the soil becomes and on its pH. Manganese dissolves more readily when a soil stays flooded and short of oxygen, so differences in how the fields were watered at the three locations are the most likely reason for the difference. Reports on these minerals in the aromatic landraces of West Bengal are few. Singh et al. (2022) found wide cultivar differences in mineral content among the pigmented rices of north-east India, and Naveed et al. (2023) recorded that the ash and mineral contents of brown Basmati stayed steady through six months of storage while the antioxidant fraction fell, which agrees with the stability of the minerals seen here.

sec: 4.7 Amino acid profile of freshly harvested grain
text: The amino acid profile was worked out on freshly harvested grain only. The samples drawn at 4, 8 and 12 months were not tested for these parameters. The results in this section therefore describe how location and variety affected the amino acids of fresh grain. Nothing is said about the effect of storage, because that effect was not measured. Each table gives the S1 means only, and the SEm and CD figures apply to the location and variety interaction.

sec: 4.7 Amino acid profile of freshly harvested grain
text: For fourteen of the fifteen amino acids the effect of location was not significant. Proline was the only exception. Varietal differences, by contrast, were highly significant for every amino acid tested. Put simply, the amino acid make-up of these landraces is decided mainly by the seed and hardly at all by the district in which it is grown.

sec: 4.7 Amino acid profile of freshly harvested grain
text: Gobindabhog held the most of thirteen of the fifteen amino acids, with Radhunipagal next and Kalojira last. There were two exceptions. Kalojira held far more cysteine than either of the others, and it came second for tyrosine. Cysteine and tyrosine were barely detectable in Radhunipagal, at 0.0017 and 0.0014 mg/100 mg, which are figures at the very bottom of what the method can measure.

The effect of location on histidine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Nadia recorded 0.1098 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.1088 mg/100 mg and Birbhum/Howrah 0.1087 mg/100 mg.

The three landraces were clearly different, the varietal effect reaching the 1% level. Gobindabhog carried the highest amount, 0.1438 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal followed at 0.1075 mg/100 mg, and the smallest amount was in Kalojira at 0.0760 mg/100 mg.

No significant location by variety interaction arose, so each landrace behaved alike at all three sites. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 0.1451 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.0753 mg/100 mg. This parameter was measured only in fresh grain, so no storage interaction is reported.

Histidine is an essential amino acid. It is needed for growth and for making haemoglobin, and it is the building block from which the body makes histamine. The three locations gave almost identical readings, from 0.1098 mg/100 mg at Nadia down to 0.1087 mg/100 mg at Birbhum and Howrah. The whole spread was 0.0011 mg/100 mg, which is far too small to matter. Grain protein composition is laid down by the seed rather than by the soil, so this result is expected. Gobindabhog is therefore the better of the three on this count. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) placed histidine in rice protein at 1.0 to 3.8% of the total. A grower or a buyer can therefore rely on Gobindabhog to be the richest in histidine wherever it is grown in West Bengal.

The effect of location on serine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.3905 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3897 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.3889 mg/100 mg.

Clear differences separated the landraces, and the effect of variety was highly significant. The largest quantity was in Gobindabhog, at 0.5544 mg/100 mg. Next was Radhunipagal with 0.3432 mg/100 mg, while Kalojira carried the least at 0.2715 mg/100 mg.

The location by variety term fell short of significance; every landrace acted the same way in all three districts. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.5563 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.2712 mg/100 mg. No storage samples were assayed for this character; storage interactions are therefore absent.

Serine is a non-essential amino acid, which means the body can make it. It takes part in building fats and cell membranes and is a starting point for making glycine and cysteine. The three locations were within 0.0016 mg/100 mg of one another, from 0.3905 mg/100 mg at Birbhum and Howrah to 0.3889 mg/100 mg at Nadia, and the difference was not significant. Gobindabhog held roughly twice the serine of Kalojira, at 0.5544 against 0.2715 mg/100 mg, with Radhunipagal at 0.3432 mg/100 mg. Serine is plentiful in the glutelin fraction, which makes up most of rice storage protein. A landrace with more storage protein will therefore show more serine. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported that glutelin accounts for 79 to 83% of the protein of milled rice, so its amino acids largely set the profile of the whole grain.

The effect of location on arginine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.3113 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3110 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.3100 mg/100 mg.

The landraces differed clearly, with a highly significant varietal effect. Gobindabhog ranked highest with 0.4205 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal took second place at 0.3102 mg/100 mg and Kalojira the last at 0.2016 mg/100 mg.

Location and variety did not interact significantly, indicating uniform landrace behaviour across the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.4223 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Nadia with 0.1985 mg/100 mg. Since the determination was confined to fresh grain, storage terms do not arise.

Arginine is conditionally essential, meaning healthy adults can make enough of it but infants and people under stress cannot. It helps the body clear waste nitrogen and is needed to make nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels. The three locations differed by only 0.0013 mg/100 mg and the effect was not significant. Birbhum and Howrah gave 0.3113 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3110 and Nadia 0.3100. Gobindabhog held 0.4205 mg/100 mg, more than double Kalojira at 0.2016, with Radhunipagal at 0.3102 mg/100 mg. Arginine is concentrated in the embryo and the outer layers of the grain. The way each landrace mills will therefore affect how much of it survives into the polished rice. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) listed arginine among the amino acids that are plentiful in the prolamin fraction of rice.

The effect of location on glycine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Nadia recorded 0.4098 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.4092 mg/100 mg and Birbhum/Howrah 0.4086 mg/100 mg.

Marked differences appeared between landraces; variety was highly significant. Highest of all was Gobindabhog at 0.5587 mg/100 mg. Behind it came Radhunipagal at 0.3886 mg/100 mg, with Kalojira lowest at 0.2804 mg/100 mg.

Since the interaction was not significant, the landraces responded identically at each of the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.5603 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.2794 mg/100 mg. Storage was not sampled for this character, so no term involving it appears.

Glycine is the smallest and simplest amino acid. It is a major part of collagen and it helps the liver clear toxins. The three locations were separated by 0.0012 mg/100 mg, which was not significant. Nadia gave 0.4098 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.4092 and Birbhum and Howrah 0.4086. Gobindabhog held 0.5587 mg/100 mg against 0.2804 in Kalojira, so almost exactly double, with Radhunipagal at 0.3886 mg/100 mg. The doubling seen here for glycine, serine and histidine alike points to a general difference in the quantity of storage protein. It does not point to any special feature of one amino acid. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported glycine among the amino acids plentiful in the prolamin fraction. Kamjijam et al. (2020) mapped it to the germ and outer layers of the rice grain.

The effect of location on aspartic acid content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.5469 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.5466 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.5464 mg/100 mg.

The three landraces were clearly different, the varietal effect reaching the 1% level. Gobindabhog carried the highest amount, 0.6690 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal followed at 0.5183 mg/100 mg, and the smallest amount was in Kalojira at 0.4526 mg/100 mg.

No significant location by variety interaction arose, so each landrace behaved alike at all three sites. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.6699 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 0.4521 mg/100 mg. This parameter was measured only in fresh grain, so no storage interaction is reported.

Aspartic acid is a non-essential amino acid that takes part in the urea cycle and in the energy pathways of the cell. Along with glutamic acid it contributes to the savoury taste of cooked food. The three locations were within 0.0005 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was not significant. The coefficient of variation was the second lowest of all fifteen amino acids at 1.37%, which shows how repeatable the measurement was. The spread between landraces was narrower here than for most other amino acids. Gobindabhog held 0.6690 mg/100 mg, Radhunipagal 0.5183 and Kalojira 0.4526, so Gobindabhog exceeded Kalojira by 48% rather than the doubling seen elsewhere. Kamjijam et al. (2020) mapped aspartic acid to the germ of the rice grain and found it among the amino acids present in the largest quantity.

The effect of location on glutamic acid content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Nadia recorded 1.2610 mg/100 mg, Birbhum/Howrah 1.2604 mg/100 mg and Purba Bardhaman 1.2600 mg/100 mg.

Clear differences separated the landraces, and the effect of variety was highly significant. The largest quantity was in Gobindabhog, at 1.4690 mg/100 mg. Next was Radhunipagal with 1.1983 mg/100 mg, while Kalojira carried the least at 1.1141 mg/100 mg.

The location by variety term fell short of significance; every landrace acted the same way in all three districts. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 1.4694 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 1.1130 mg/100 mg. No storage samples were assayed for this character; storage interactions are therefore absent.

Glutamic acid was the most plentiful amino acid in all three landraces. It is the main amino acid of cereal storage protein and it is what gives cooked rice much of its savoury taste. The three locations differed by only 0.0010 mg/100 mg, which was not significant. The coefficient of variation was the lowest of all the amino acids at 0.64%. Glutamic acid makes up the mainstay of the glutelin fraction. Its share therefore cannot vary greatly from one landrace to another. Renuka et al. (2022) showed that it works together with proline and ornithine as a precursor of 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. The extremes were Gobindabhog at Birbhum and Howrah with 1.4694 mg/100 mg and Kalojira at the same location with 1.1130 mg/100 mg, which shows that the landrace mattered and the location did not.

The effect of location on threonine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Purba Bardhaman recorded 0.2013 mg/100 mg, Birbhum/Howrah 0.2012 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.2012 mg/100 mg.

The landraces differed clearly, with a highly significant varietal effect. Gobindabhog ranked highest with 0.2770 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal took second place at 0.1898 mg/100 mg and Kalojira the last at 0.1368 mg/100 mg.

Location and variety did not interact significantly, indicating uniform landrace behaviour across the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 0.2778 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 0.1365 mg/100 mg. Since the determination was confined to fresh grain, storage terms do not arise.

Threonine is an essential amino acid. It is needed for making the protective mucus of the gut and for the antibodies of the immune system, and after lysine it is often the amino acid in shortest supply in cereal diets. The three locations were within 0.0001 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was not significant. Gobindabhog held 0.2770 mg/100 mg, twice the 0.1368 recorded in Kalojira, with Radhunipagal at 0.1898 mg/100 mg. Threonine is one of the limiting amino acids in a rice based diet. A doubling between landraces is therefore of real nutritional interest and marks Gobindabhog out for anyone selecting on protein quality. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) gave the threonine content of rice protein as 3.15 to 4.43%. They listed threonine with lysine and tryptophan as the amino acids in shortest supply in rice.

The effect of location on alanine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Purba Bardhaman recorded 0.4512 mg/100 mg, Birbhum/Howrah 0.4501 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.4493 mg/100 mg.

Marked differences appeared between landraces; variety was highly significant. Highest of all was Gobindabhog at 0.6596 mg/100 mg. Behind it came Radhunipagal at 0.4171 mg/100 mg, with Kalojira lowest at 0.2739 mg/100 mg.

Since the interaction was not significant, the landraces responded identically at each of the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.6604 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Nadia with 0.2721 mg/100 mg. Storage was not sampled for this character, so no term involving it appears.

Alanine is a non-essential amino acid. It carries nitrogen from the muscles to the liver and takes part in the cycle that turns protein into glucose when the body needs energy. The three locations were separated by 0.0019 mg/100 mg, which was not significant. Gobindabhog held 0.6596 mg/100 mg against 0.2739 in Kalojira, a difference of 141%, which was the widest relative gap of any amino acid other than cysteine and tyrosine. Radhunipagal held 0.4171 mg/100 mg. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) described the amino acid balance of rice as uneven. Alanine is among the amino acids present in the largest quantity, at 4 to 11% of the total. Much of it sits in the prolamin fraction. The interaction was not significant and the ranking held everywhere.
The effect of location on proline content of freshly harvested grain was significant. Purba Bardhaman recorded 0.3000 mg/100 mg, Nadia 0.2967 mg/100 mg and Birbhum/Howrah 0.2954 mg/100 mg.

The three landraces were clearly different, the varietal effect reaching the 1% level. Gobindabhog carried the highest amount, 0.4311 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal followed at 0.2674 mg/100 mg, and the smallest amount was in Kalojira at 0.1935 mg/100 mg.

No significant location by variety interaction arose, so each landrace behaved alike at all three sites. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.4333 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Nadia with 0.1919 mg/100 mg. This parameter was measured only in fresh grain, so no storage interaction is reported.

Proline deserves particular attention in a study of aromatic rice. Apart from its role in building protein, it is the compound from which the plant makes 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the substance responsible for the characteristic smell of aromatic rice. This ranking is worth pausing over, because it runs opposite to the aroma scores, where Kalojira ranked first by a wide margin and Gobindabhog came second. Luo et al. (2020) showed this directly. The two therefore need not agree, and the result is a reminder that a high total proline content does not by itself promise a fragrant grain. Itani et al. (2004) traced such location differences in aroma back to how much precursor the grain can draw on while it fills. Imran et al. (2023) reviewed the recent work on this pathway.

The effect of location on cysteine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Nadia recorded 0.8666 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.8664 mg/100 mg and Birbhum/Howrah 0.8657 mg/100 mg.

Clear differences separated the landraces, and the effect of variety was highly significant. The largest quantity was in Kalojira, at 1.6729 mg/100 mg. Next was Gobindabhog with 0.9240 mg/100 mg, while Radhunipagal carried the least at 0.0017 mg/100 mg.

The location by variety term fell short of significance; every landrace acted the same way in all three districts. The highest single combination was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 1.6744 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.0010 mg/100 mg. No storage samples were assayed for this character; storage interactions are therefore absent.

Cysteine carries a sulphur group, which makes it unlike the other amino acids measured here. Kalojira therefore held nearly a thousand times more cysteine than Radhunipagal. It should be confirmed against the raw chromatograms before the table is finalised, because a failure to detect a peak looks the same as a genuine absence. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported cysteine in rice protein over a range of 0.13 to 3.42%. A landrace difference of this kind is therefore not impossible. The high cysteine of Kalojira fits with its position as the landrace with the greatest antioxidant capacity, since the sulphur group contributes to that property. Cysteine is the amino acid that forms the sulphur bridges responsible for protein becoming less soluble as rice ages (Chrastil and Zarins, 1992), so Kalojira may be the landrace most prone to that change during long storage.

The effect of location on tyrosine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Purba Bardhaman recorded 0.2821 mg/100 mg, Birbhum/Howrah 0.2819 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.2807 mg/100 mg.

The landraces differed clearly, with a highly significant varietal effect. Gobindabhog ranked highest with 0.5965 mg/100 mg. Kalojira took second place at 0.2467 mg/100 mg and Radhunipagal the last at 0.0014 mg/100 mg.

The location and variety interaction was significant. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.5973 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman with 0.0007 mg/100 mg. Since the determination was confined to fresh grain, storage terms do not arise.

Tyrosine is an aromatic amino acid. The body uses it to make several signalling compounds and the pigment melanin, and in plants it is the starting point for a range of phenolic compounds. The three locations were within 0.0014 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was not significant. Gobindabhog held the most tyrosine at 0.5965 mg/100 mg, followed by Kalojira at 0.2467, while Radhunipagal again recorded a trace value of 0.0014 mg/100 mg. As with cysteine, the near absence in Radhunipagal is extreme enough to deserve checking against the raw output before it is reported as a real finding. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) gave a range of 0.81 to 6.0% for tyrosine in milled rice. A large varietal spread is therefore expected. The spread recorded here is wider still.

The effect of location on valine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.3459 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3456 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.3448 mg/100 mg.

Marked differences appeared between landraces; variety was highly significant. Highest of all was Gobindabhog at 0.4772 mg/100 mg. Behind it came Radhunipagal at 0.3316 mg/100 mg, with Kalojira lowest at 0.2276 mg/100 mg.

Location and variety did not interact significantly, indicating uniform landrace behaviour across the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.4787 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 0.2275 mg/100 mg. Storage was not sampled for this character, so no term involving it appears.

Valine is an essential branched chain amino acid. Together with leucine and isoleucine it is used directly by muscle for energy and for repair. The three locations differed by 0.0011 mg/100 mg, which was not significant. Gobindabhog held 0.4772 mg/100 mg, Radhunipagal 0.3316 and Kalojira 0.2276 mg/100 mg, so Gobindabhog held 110% more than Kalojira. Valine is essential and must come from the diet. This difference therefore has practical value where rice makes up most of the protein intake. Sui et al. (2023) mapped the genes controlling branched chain amino acid content in 422 rice accessions. They found the trait to be governed by many genes of small effect. That fits the steady varietal differences seen here. The interaction was not significant. The extremes were Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman with 0.4787 mg/100 mg and Kalojira at the same location with 0.2275 mg/100 mg.

The effect of location on isoleucine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Purba Bardhaman recorded 0.2113 mg/100 mg, Birbhum/Howrah 0.2111 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.2104 mg/100 mg.

The three landraces were clearly different, the varietal effect reaching the 1% level. Gobindabhog carried the highest amount, 0.2874 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal followed at 0.2108 mg/100 mg, and the smallest amount was in Kalojira at 0.1345 mg/100 mg.

The location and variety interaction was significant. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.2883 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 0.1340 mg/100 mg. This parameter was measured only in fresh grain, so no storage interaction is reported.

Isoleucine is the second of the three essential branched chain amino acids. It supports muscle repair, helps regulate blood sugar and takes part in the formation of haemoglobin. The three locations were within 0.0009 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was not significant. Gobindabhog held 0.2874 mg/100 mg, Radhunipagal 0.2108 and Kalojira 0.1345 mg/100 mg. Isoleucine was the least plentiful of the three branched chain amino acids in all three landraces. That is the usual pattern in cereal protein. Sui et al. (2023) reported the same ranking across a wide panel of rice accessions and identified two candidate genes governing isoleucine content. The interaction was significant, the second of only two amino acids for which this happened, though the ranking of the landraces stayed the same at all three locations.

The effect of location on leucine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Nadia recorded 0.4069 mg/100 mg, Birbhum/Howrah 0.4062 mg/100 mg and Purba Bardhaman 0.4057 mg/100 mg.

Clear differences separated the landraces, and the effect of variety was highly significant. The largest quantity was in Gobindabhog, at 0.5502 mg/100 mg. Next was Radhunipagal with 0.4060 mg/100 mg, while Kalojira carried the least at 0.2625 mg/100 mg.

Since the interaction was not significant, the landraces responded identically at each of the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.5523 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 0.2618 mg/100 mg. No storage samples were assayed for this character; storage interactions are therefore absent.

Leucine is the third and most active of the branched chain amino acids. It is the strongest dietary trigger for muscle protein building and it helps regulate blood sugar. The three locations were within 0.0012 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was not significant. Gobindabhog held 0.5502 mg/100 mg, Radhunipagal 0.4060 and Kalojira 0.2625 mg/100 mg. Leucine was the most plentiful of the three branched chain amino acids in every landrace. This agrees with the general composition of cereal protein and with the wide panel of accessions studied by Sui et al. (2023). Gobindabhog held 110% more than Kalojira. The interaction was not significant and the ranking held at every location. The extremes were Gobindabhog at Birbhum and Howrah with 0.5523 mg/100 mg and Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman with 0.2618 mg/100 mg.

The effect of location on phenylalanine content of freshly harvested grain was not significant, so the three locations gave similar reading. Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.2426 mg/100 mg, Nadia 0.2404 mg/100 mg and Purba Bardhaman 0.2403 mg/100 mg.

The landraces differed clearly, with a highly significant varietal effect. Gobindabhog ranked highest with 0.3598 mg/100 mg. Radhunipagal took second place at 0.2301 mg/100 mg and Kalojira the last at 0.1333 mg/100 mg.

No significant location by variety interaction arose, so each landrace behaved alike at all three sites. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.3626 mg/100 mg and the lowest was Kalojira at Nadia with 0.1324 mg/100 mg. Since the determination was confined to fresh grain, storage terms do not arise.

Phenylalanine is an essential aromatic amino acid. The phenolic compounds of the grain are built from this amino acid, so the two results together suggest that Kalojira diverts a larger share of its phenylalanine into phenolic production rather than accumulating the amino acid itself. The order of the three landraces for amino acids matches their order for soluble protein, with Gobindabhog ahead of both the others. Sui et al. (2023) likewise found grain amino acid content to be strongly genotype-dependent in a panel of 422 rice accessions. This is normal for cereal grain, because the main storage protein of rice is rich in it. The two results sit well together and support the view of Itani et al. (2004) that location differences in aroma trace back to how much precursor is available while the grain is filling.

sec: 4.8 Correlation, principal component and cluster analysis
text: The analysis of variance reported in sections 4.1 to 4.7 treats each parameter alone. That approach answers the question of whether a given factor changed a given trait, but it cannot say how the traits move together or which treatments are alike overall. Three further analyses were therefore carried out to answer those questions, namely correlation analysis, principal component analysis and hierarchical cluster analysis.

sec: 4.8 Correlation, principal component and cluster analysis
text: All three were based on the thirty six location by variety by storage treatment means, pooled over the two years, for the twenty three parameters in which storage was assayed. The fifteen amino acids were left out because they were measured only in fresh grain and so are not available for all thirty six treatments. It should be kept in mind that these analyses use treatment means rather than individual replicate values, so the coefficients describe how the treatment means move together and are not estimates of correlation among individual observations.

sec: 4.8 Correlation, principal component and cluster analysis
text: The multivariate approach used here follows current practice. Abdelsalam et al. (2025) combined physical, cooking, nutritional and micronutrient characters of rice cultivars in a single principal component and cluster analysis and showed that the integrated profile separates cultivars more reliably than any single trait, which is the reason the treatment combinations were grouped on all characters together in the present study.

The thirty six treatment means were used to work out how the twenty three quality parameters move together. Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated for all 253 possible pairs. With 36 pairs of values and 34 degrees of freedom, a coefficient of 0.329 or larger is significant at the 5% level and one of 0.424 or larger at the 1% level. Eighty seven of the 253 pairs, or 34% of them, cleared the 5% mark. The full matrix is shown in Figure 4.1, where only the significant coefficients are printed.

The strongest link of all was between total phenol and total flavonoid, at r = +0.966. This is close to a one to one relationship and it is exactly what chemistry predicts, since flavonoids are one family within the phenolic group and are counted twice, once in each test. In practical terms this means one of the two tests carries almost no information the other does not, and a laboratory short of time could measure either one alone with little loss.

Total phenol was also strongly tied to antioxidant capacity at r = +0.896, and flavonoid to antioxidant capacity at r = +0.888. Together these three form a tight block. The phenolic compounds in the grain are the main thing doing the antioxidant work, so a landrace or a location that is rich in one will be rich in all three.

Aroma was tied to fat at r = +0.894, which is one of the more useful findings to come out of the correlation work. Both fell by about a third over the year and they fell together, treatment by treatment. This supports the argument made in section 4.3 that the two are causally linked, because the products of fat breakdown give old rice its stale smell and work against whatever aroma is left. Aroma was also tied to antioxidant capacity at r = +0.854 and to phenol at r = +0.796, so the whole group of desirable qualities rises and falls as one.

The strongest negative link was between amylose and soluble protein at r = -0.886. Starch and protein compete for the same room inside the endosperm, so grain rich in one tends to be poor in the other. Chattopadhyay et al. (2018) reported the same negative link between grain protein and amylose in rice. Amylose was also negatively tied to antioxidant capacity at r = -0.749 and to fat at r = -0.687, because amylose increased during storage while these two fell.

Among the minerals, copper and manganese were negatively linked at r = -0.764 while copper and zinc were positively linked at r = +0.685. Copper and zinc are taken up by partly shared routes in the plant, which explains the positive tie, while manganese behaves differently because its availability depends so heavily on how flooded and how reduced the soil is.

Two links matter for milling practice. Milling percentage was tied to total starch at r = +0.721 and hulling to total starch at r = +0.660. Grain that is well filled with starch is denser and stands up better to polishing. Head rice recovery was tied to ash at r = +0.640 and negatively to phytic acid at r = -0.540, and to moisture at r = +0.520.

Taken as a whole the correlation matrix says something important for anyone planning future work on these landraces. The desirable traits form one tightly linked group that declines together during storage. These are aroma, fat, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant capacity and soluble protein. Amylose moves against them. A single well chosen measurement from within that group, such as antioxidant capacity or aroma, would give a good indication of the rest and would save a great deal of laboratory effort in a screening programme.

Principal component analysis was carried out on the same matrix of thirty six treatment means and twenty three parameters. Because the parameters are measured in very different units, ranging from colour readings in the hundreds down to mineral concentrations in thousandths of a milligram, every parameter was first standardised to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This gives each parameter equal weight and stops the large numbers from dominating the result.

Six components had an eigenvalue above one and together they accounted for 83.82% of the total variation. The first two alone accounted for 50.61% and the first three for 62.99%. The scree plot in Figure 4.2 shows the sharp drop after the second component, which is the usual sign that the first two carry most of the useful information.

The first component explained 31.23% of the variation and had an eigenvalue of 7.184. It loaded heavily and positively on aroma (+0.939), antioxidant capacity (+0.910), total phenol (+0.893), fat (+0.881), total flavonoid (+0.871) and soluble protein (+0.805), and heavily and negatively on amylose (-0.713) and total colour difference (-0.604). This is the storage axis. Every trait that falls during storage loads positive and every trait that rises loads negative. Reading the biplot in Figure 4.3 from right to left is therefore the same as reading the storage period from fresh paddy to twelve months.

The second component explained 19.37% of the variation and had an eigenvalue of 4.456. It loaded most heavily and positively on phytic acid (+0.898), iron (+0.481) and L* (+0.461), and negatively on head rice recovery (-0.755), a* (-0.621), ash (-0.563) and amylose (-0.562). This is largely a varietal axis. Gobindabhog held the most phytic acid and the most iron and sits high on this component. Kalojira had the best head rice recovery and the most ash and sits low.

The third component explained 12.39% and separated the minerals from everything else. It loaded positively on zinc (+0.868) and copper (+0.789) and negatively on manganese (-0.747). Since storage had no effect on any of the minerals, this component is picking up differences between locations in soil mineral supply.

The biplot in Figure 4.3 makes the structure easy to read. The twelve Kalojira points sit together on the right and low, showing high aroma, high phenolic content and high head rice recovery. Within each landrace the four storage points run from right to left in order, from fresh paddy through to twelve months, and the length of that track shows how much the landrace changed. The arrows for aroma, fat, phenol, flavonoid and antioxidant capacity all point the same way and lie close together. This confirms the tight correlation already noted. The amylose arrow points the opposite way, and the phytic acid arrow points nearly at right angles to both groups, which indicates that phytic acid varies independently of the aroma and phenolic block.

The practical value of this analysis is that it reduces twenty three separate measurements to two readable dimensions that between them capture half the variation. A treatment can be placed on the biplot and its whole quality profile read off at a glance, which is far quicker than comparing twenty three tables one at a time.

Hierarchical cluster analysis was carried out on the standardised data using Ward's minimum variance method with Euclidean distance. This method joins together the treatments that are most alike and builds up a tree, shown as the dendrogram in Figure 4.4. The cophenetic correlation was 0.503, which is moderate and indicates that the tree gives a fair but not perfect picture of the distances between treatments.

Cutting the tree into four groups gave clusters of 12, 4, 7 and 13 treatments. What stands out simultaneously is that the grouping follows the landrace far more closely than it follows either the location or the storage period.

Cluster 1 held exactly the twelve Kalojira treatments and nothing else, that is, all three locations at all four storage periods. Not a single Kalojira treatment fell outside it and no other landrace fell inside it. This cluster recorded the highest aroma (2.51), the highest total phenol (0.7812 mg GAE/g), the highest antioxidant capacity (40.26 mg TE/100 g), the highest head rice recovery (67.07%), the highest hulling (77.52%) and the lowest phytic acid (196.07 mg/100 g). It is the best cluster on almost every count that matters, and it is defined purely by genotype.

Cluster 2 held the four Radhunipagal treatments from Nadia. It is small and tight, and it is set apart by mineral content rather than by anything else. It recorded much the highest zinc at 1.37 ppm, which is nearly three times the level of the other clusters, along with the highest ash at 1.16% and the highest copper. This shows that one landrace at one location can behave quite unlike the same landrace elsewhere, which is the clearest possible confirmation of the location and variety interactions reported throughout this chapter.

Cluster 3 held seven treatments, all of them Gobindabhog or Radhunipagal from the middle and later storage periods, mostly from Purba Bardhaman. This is the deteriorated group. It recorded the lowest aroma (1.78), the lowest total phenol (0.4380 mg GAE/g), the lowest antioxidant capacity (22.33 mg TE/100 g) and the lowest ash. It shows what happens when a landrace with only moderate quality to begin with is grown at the weakest location and then held for eight to twelve months.

Cluster 4 held thirteen treatments, made up mainly of fresh and early stored Gobindabhog together with the earlier Radhunipagal samples. It recorded the highest phytic acid at 373.41 mg/100 g and the highest iron at 0.48 ppm, with moderate values for most other traits.

Three lessons come out of the clustering. First, genotype was the strongest single force shaping overall quality, since Kalojira separated completely from the other two landraces before any other division appeared in the tree. Second, storage was the next strongest force, since within Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal the fresh and early samples separated from the late ones. Third, location mattered least of the three on the whole, but it was decisive in the one case of Radhunipagal at Nadia, which broke away as a cluster of its own on the strength of its mineral content.

For a breeding or a marketing programme the message is straightforward. Choose Kalojira for aroma, phenolics and milling outturn. Choose Radhunipagal from Nadia if mineral content is the goal. Avoid holding Gobindabhog or Radhunipagal from Purba Bardhaman beyond eight months, because that is the combination that lands in the poorest cluster.

The place of growing mattered for nearly every trait measured. Birbhum and Howrah gave the best milling percentage, head rice recovery, total phenol, total flavonoid, antioxidant capacity, iron and phytic acid. Nadia gave the best hulling, soluble protein, fat, copper and zinc. Purba Bardhaman was the weakest location for most of the traits that decide nutritional value.

Kalojira came out as the best all round landrace. It ranked highest for hulling, milling, head rice recovery, total starch, amylose, fat, ash, aroma, total phenol, total flavonoid and antioxidant capacity. Gobindabhog was better for soluble protein, grain shape, iron and thirteen of the fifteen amino acids. Radhunipagal ranked highest only for zinc and was the lowest performer for most milling and nutritional traits.

Storage pulled quality in two directions simultaneously. Milling improved as the grain aged, with head rice recovery gaining 2.13 percentage points up to 8 months, and amylose increased by 12.8% over the year. Against these gains, aroma fell by 31.7%, soluble protein by 41.4%, fat by 31.3%, total phenol by 52.4%, total flavonoid by 37.3% and antioxidant capacity by 62.7%.

Copper, iron, zinc and manganese did not change at all during storage, while phytic acid fell by 40.0% in the same period. Because phytic acid is what blocks the body from absorbing iron and zinc, the balance between them improved steadily as the grain aged. Aged grain should therefore give up its minerals more readily than fresh grain, even though it holds no more of them.

The interactions add three lessons that the main effects alone would hide. First, for the milling traits and for aroma the order of the landraces held firm at every location, so the choice of landrace can be made once for the whole of West Bengal. Second, for soluble protein, ash and all four minerals the order of the landraces changed from location to location, so no landrace can be recommended for these traits without naming the district. Third, for aroma, fat and amylose all three landraces changed at nearly the same rate during storage, which means one storage rule will serve all of them.

Taken together, a storage period of four to eight months is the best compromise for these landraces. Within that window most of the milling gain from ageing has been won while the loss of aroma and health giving compounds is still moderate. Holding the grain beyond eight months in ordinary conditions costs a great deal of the aroma and antioxidant value that these landraces are paid a premium for, and none of it can be obtained back.

The seven products in this experiment were prepared from nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal, with Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar, included as the control. Each product was laid out in a completely randomised design with three replications and repeated over two years. The two years were analysed together as a pooled design, with year as a fixed effect and cultivar as a random effect. The model was Yijk = μ + Yi + Tj + (YT)ij + eijk, and the degrees of freedom were year 1, cultivar 9, year by cultivar 9, error 40 and total 59.

The results are set out in two parts. Part A covers the four cooked products, table rice, khichdi, pulao and payash, and Part B the three processed products, popped rice, puffed rice and flattened rice. Within each part every attribute is presented once for the group, with all the products of that part set together in one table and one figure, both giving the means pooled over the two years. Means were separated at the 5% level and are reported with letter groupings; a cultivar is taken to differ from the control only where the two share no letter. Throughout,  denotes significance at 1%, * at 5% and NS non-significance. Since a high value is favourable for some attributes and a low value for others, each cultivar is compared with the control in the direction appropriate to that attribute.

Each part closes with a composite quality score index, a check on the weights of that index using principal component analysis, a cluster analysis of the cultivar and product combinations, and a conclusion. Tables and figures are numbered continuously through both parts.

Amylose content determines the firmness and separateness of the cooked grain. A higher content gives a firmer, drier grain that holds its shape, and a lower content a softer, stickier one. In table rice the values ranged from 15.63 in Harinakhuri to 19.82% in Kalojira. The control recorded 17.19%, 8 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalojira was the most favourable. Tulaipanji recorded the highest value in khichdi at 9.11% and Kalonunia the lowest at 6.14%. Against 6.77% for the control, 3 cultivars exceeded it, and Tulaipanji was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 16.30 and 20.57%, with the control at 18.35%. Here 2 cultivars exceeded the control, with Kalojira the highest. In payash the values ranged from 16.74 in Harinakhuri to 21.02% in Kalojira. Against the control at 18.91%, 3 cultivars ranked higher, Kalojira being the highest. The means are given in Table 4.40 and plotted in Fig. 4.5.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. The year term was significant in 1 products and the year by cultivar term in 1, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.91 and 3.19%, so the trial was precise. Amylose is laid down by granule bound starch synthase I at the Waxy locus, and cultivars differ in the allele they carry. Cooking disorganises the granule but does not alter the amount of amylose present.

This agrees with what has been reported before. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported apparent amylose decides eating and processing behaviour, Tian et al. (2018) observed crystallinity and digestibility fall without amylose changing. Cheng et al. (2019) recorded heat and moisture rebuild the matrix into a firmer gel, Devi and Badwaik (2022) showed amylose explains most of the varietal difference in cooking. The most favourable entry differed between products. Kalojira and Tulaipanji each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Starch is the energy supplying fraction of the grain and the basis of its texture. A higher value indicates a well filled endosperm and good recovery of the edible fraction. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in table rice at 28.07% and Kataribhog the lowest at 20.49%. The control gave 23.45%; 5 cultivars exceeded it, Radhunipagal most markedly. For khichdi the values lay between 34.24 and 42.72%, with the control at 38.36%. Lal Badshabhog ranked first, and 6 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In pulao the values ranged from 20.66 in Dudeshwar to 28.51% in Kataribhog. The control gave 20.66%; 8 cultivars exceeded that value and Kataribhog ranked first. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in payash at 24.22% and Tulaipanji the lowest at 16.57%. Relative to 19.22% for the control, 4 cultivars were higher, with Kalonunia the best among them. Table 4.41 gives the means and Fig. 4.6 shows them. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. The year effect was not significant in any product, though the year by cultivar interaction was significant in 2, so in those products the difference between cultivars was not of the same magnitude in both years. The coefficient of variation ran from 2.30 to 2.68%, which points to reliable measurement.

Starch content depends on how efficiently assimilate was moved into the endosperm during grain filling. In the prepared product it is further affected by the loss of low molecular weight material and by the water taken up in cooking. Earlier work points the same way. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted starch makes up about nine tenths of milled rice by dry weight, Tian et al. (2018) concluded the residual starch is swollen and less crystalline. Iqbal et al. (2021) demonstrated restructured starch resists digestion, Cheng et al. (2019) found how far the starch gelatinises drives texture and digestion.
The leading cultivar changed with the product, Kalonunia, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Protein is the main nutritional contribution of rice after energy, and it also firms the cooked grain through disulphide bonding. For table rice the values lay between 2.56 and 3.36%, with the control at 2.56%. 3 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Radhunipagal ranked highest. In khichdi the values ranged from 16.49 in Kalojira to 18.23% in Gobindabhog. The control recorded 16.74%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Gobindabhog gave the most favourable value. Kalojira recorded the highest value in pulao at 4.35% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 3.62%. The control recorded 3.62%. 2 cultivars exceeded it and Kalojira ranked most favourable. For payash the values lay between 5.39 and 6.57%, with the control at 5.39%. Here one cultivar exceeded the control and Kalonunia ranked highest. The values appear in Table 4.42, with Fig. 4.7 showing the same data.

Only 3 of the 4 products showed a significant cultivar effect. Year and its interaction with cultivar both fell short of significance, so the order was the same in each year. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 6.60 and 8.64%. Most of the protein is glutelin stored in protein bodies beneath the aleurone, and the amount depends on the nitrogen moved into the grain during filling. Cooking does not alter it.

Published work points in the same direction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported total protein is unchanged by hydrothermal treatment. Cheng et al. (2019) observed disulphide cross links raise firmness, and Akter et al. (2025) recorded protein rose from 6.68 to 9.42% after treatment; Iqbal et al. (2021) found the protein network controls enzyme access to starch. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Kalonunia and Radhunipagal, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Soluble protein is the fraction that remains extractable, and therefore digestible, after cooking. A higher value indicates that heat has not aggregated the protein. In table rice the values ranged from 0.47 in Dudeshwar to 0.61% in Radhunipagal. With the control at 0.47%, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Radhunipagal was the best. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 1.64% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 1.37%. Against 1.37% for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded it, and Gobindabhog was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 0.53 and 0.90%, with the control at 0.53%. 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Tulaipanji being the highest among them. In payash the values ranged from 1.19 in Lal Badshabhog to 1.56% in Gobindabhog. The control recorded 1.31%, 6 cultivars exceeded it, and Gobindabhog was the most favourable. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.43 and illustrated in Fig. 4.8. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. Neither year nor the year by cultivar term reached significance; ranking was unchanged between years. With coefficients of variation of 1.32 to 3.62%, the experiment was well controlled.

Heat ruptures the protein bodies and then cross links the released chains through disulphide bonds, which lowers the extractable fraction. Cultivars richer in cysteine lose more. The same pattern has been reported before. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed solubility changes while total protein does not, Cheng et al. (2019) noted cross linking lowers the extractable fraction. Kabir et al. (2025) concluded treatment changes how protein and bound phenolics associate, Roy et al. (2019) demonstrated solubility falls as steam and soaking become more severe.
Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Tulaipanji each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Lipid is located in the germ and aleurone and carries the fat soluble vitamins and the aroma compounds. A higher content is better, although excess lipid shortens shelf life. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in table rice at 0.34% and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.23%. Against 0.32% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal was the most favourable entry. For khichdi the values lay between 10.78 and 13.25%, with the control at 13.25%. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In pulao the values ranged from 3.06 in Gobindabhog to 3.53% in Kalojira. The control recorded 3.49%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalojira gave the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in payash at 7.06% and Gobindabhog the lowest at 6.70%. Against 7.06% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. Table 4.44 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.9.

The cultivar effect was significant in 2 products out of 4. Year mattered in 1 products and the year by cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. The coefficient of variation stayed within 2.62 to 11.44%, a sign of good precision. Lipid is stored as triacylglycerol in the germ and aleurone, so the value reflects both the size of these tissues in the cultivar and the extent of milling.

Earlier reports support this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found lipid sits in germ and aleurone and oxidises readily, Hu et al. (2019) reported moving water inside the kernel shifts the lipid bearing tissues. Devi and Badwaik (2022) observed traditional cultivars differ widely in proximate composition, Oliveira et al. (2026) recorded milling is the main route by which the outer layers are lost. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Dudeshwar, Kalojira and Radhunipagal ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Ash is the residue remaining after ignition and represents the total inorganic contribution of the grain. For table rice the values lay between 0.13 and 0.43%, with the control at 0.43%. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In khichdi the values ranged from 1.94 in Radhatilak to 2.39% in Dudeshwar. The control recorded 2.39%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in pulao at 1.08% and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.81%. Against 1.08% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 1.24 and 1.60%, with the control at 1.60%. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. The data are presented in Table 4.45 and plotted in Fig. 4.10. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. The year effect was not significant in any product, though the year by cultivar interaction was significant in 2, so in those products the difference between cultivars was not of the same magnitude in both years. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 0.75 to 7.17%.

Ash follows the germ and aleurone, which carry most of the mineral matter, so cultivars with a thicker aleurone or a larger embryo give higher values. Similar results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) showed ash follows how much germ and aleurone survive, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted the spread in ash comes from the outer grain layers. Jannasch and Wang (2020) concluded the steeping medium can add to the mineral fraction, Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated ash is redistributed rather than lost on treatment.
Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value in every product of this group, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Phenolic acids are the principal antioxidants of the grain and are largely bound to the pericarp cell wall. A higher retained content in the product is better. In table rice the values ranged from 0.30 in Dudeshwar to 0.55 mg GAE/g in Kalonunia. The control recorded 0.30 mg GAE/g, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia gave the most favourable value. Lal Badshabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 6.44 mg GAE/g and Radhatilak the lowest at 5.19 mg GAE/g. Against 5.23 mg GAE/g for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, and Lal Badshabhog was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 1.69 and 3.66 mg GAE/g, with the control at 2.57 mg GAE/g. 3 cultivars exceeded the control and Kataribhog ranked first. In payash the values ranged from 10.16 in Radhunipagal to 52.32 mg GAE/g in Kalonunia. The control recorded 10.98 mg GAE/g, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia gave the most favourable value. Table 4.46 lists the means and Fig. 4.11 presents them graphically.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Significance attached to year in 3 products and to the year by cultivar interaction in 3, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.47 and 3.59%, so the trial was precise. Most phenolic acid is bound to arabinoxylan in the pericarp wall. Heat cleaves these bonds and releases it, while simultaneously degrading and leaching the free fraction, so the value recorded is the balance of the two.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Phimphilai et al. (2026) found popping and steam cooking cut total phenolics sharply, Shavandi et al. (2023) reported infrared puffing raises the extractable fraction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed heat frees ferulic and p-coumaric acid from the cell wall, Kabir et al. (2025) recorded soaking and cooking lower phenolic acids, bound exceeding free. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Kalonunia, Kataribhog and Lal Badshabhog ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Flavonoids contribute to antioxidant activity and to pericarp colour. They degrade readily on heating, so the residual content indicates how gently the grain was treated. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 0.04 mg QE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.03 mg QE/g. Against 0.03 mg QE/g for the control, 7 cultivars exceeded the control, and Gobindabhog was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 1.43 and 2.53 mg QE/g, with the control at 1.81 mg QE/g. Here 6 cultivars exceeded the control, with Kataribhog the highest. In payash the values ranged from 5.20 in Dudeshwar to 22.54 mg QE/g in Kalonunia. The control recorded 5.20 mg QE/g, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia gave the most favourable value. The means are given in Table 4.47 and plotted in Fig. 4.12. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. In 3 products the year effect was significant and in 3 the year by cultivar interaction, so the cultivars kept similar order in both years. The coefficient of variation ran from 0.68 to 2.36%, which points to reliable measurement.

Flavonoids are synthesised in the pericarp and cultivars differ in the amount deposited. They are readily destroyed by heat, so the residual content reflects both the initial level and the treatment. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Phimphilai et al. (2026) showed flavonoids break down more readily than total phenolics, Kabir et al. (2025) noted most flavonoid sits in the bound fraction. Oliveira et al. (2026) concluded long cooking can cost up to forty per cent, Devi and Badwaik (2022) demonstrated traditional cultivars differ several fold.
The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Kataribhog, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Antioxidant capacity measures the activity of the whole bioactive fraction rather than its quantity, so a higher value is desirable. For table rice the values lay between 7.20 and 8.21 mg TE/g, with the control at 7.20 mg TE/g. Lal Badshabhog ranked first, and 6 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In khichdi the values ranged from 21.84 in Kalojira to 23.98 mg TE/g in Radhunipagal. The control recorded 23.00 mg TE/g, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal gave the most favourable value. Kataribhog recorded the highest value in pulao at 9.69 mg TE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 7.63 mg TE/g. Against 7.63 mg TE/g for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kataribhog was the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 10.11 and 13.84 mg TE/g, with the control at 10.11 mg TE/g. 9 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Kalonunia ranked highest. Table 4.48 gives the means and Fig. 4.13 shows them.

The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. The year term was significant in 4 products and the year by cultivar term in 2, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 0.49 and 1.54%. Antioxidant capacity derives from the surviving phenolics and flavonoids together with browning products formed during heating, so cultivars rich in bound phenolics retain more of it.

Earlier studies report similar findings. Phimphilai et al. (2026) found capacity tracks phenolic and flavonoid content, Shavandi et al. (2023) reported activity moves with total phenolics as puffing changes. Kabir et al. (2025) observed the bound phenolics account for most of the activity, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded browning products add to measured activity. Kalonunia, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Phytic acid binds iron, zinc and calcium in the intestine and prevents their absorption. A lower content is therefore better, since it releases the very minerals the grain supplies. In table rice the values ranged from 0.06 in Kalonunia to 0.15% in Dudeshwar. Against the control at 0.15%, 8 cultivars ranked higher, Kalonunia being the highest. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in khichdi at 0.59% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.41%. Against 0.41% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 0.04 and 0.06%, with the control at 0.04%. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In payash the values ranged from 0.03 in Gobindabhog to 0.07% in Kalonunia. The control gave 0.06%; 4 cultivars exceeded that value and Gobindabhog ranked first. The values appear in Table 4.49, with Fig. 4.14 showing the same data. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. Year mattered in 1 products and the year by cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. With coefficients of variation of 2.25 to 13.09%, the experiment was well controlled.

Phytate is deposited as globoids in the aleurone during grain filling and is hydrolysed by endogenous phytase during soaking, so the residue depends on both processes. The same pattern appears in earlier reports. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed treated brown rice holds about half the phytate of untreated, Kumar et al. (2022) noted less phytate means more iron and zinc absorbed. Bhar et al. (2022) concluded cutting phytate is a main nutritional argument for processed grain, Hu et al. (2019) demonstrated germination and hydrothermal treatment work in different ways.
No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog and Kalonunia ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Copper is required for iron transport and for several enzymes, and cereals are a principal dietary source. A higher content in the product is better. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in table rice at 0.55 ppm and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.39 ppm. Against 0.55 ppm for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For khichdi the values lay between 0.30 and 0.46 ppm, with the control at 0.38 ppm. 5 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhatilak being the highest among them. In pulao the values ranged from 0.17 in Tulaipanji to 0.57 ppm in Harinakhuri. The control recorded 0.52 ppm, one cultivar exceeded the control, and Harinakhuri gave the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in payash at 0.40 ppm and Radhatilak the lowest at 0.23 ppm. Against 0.40 ppm for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.50 and illustrated in Fig. 4.15.

Significance was reached in each of the products. Significance attached to year in 4 products and to the year by cultivar interaction in 3, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. The coefficient of variation stayed within 6.00 to 6.76%, a sign of good precision. Copper is carried into the grain by COPT and HMA transporters and stored mainly in the aleurone, so cultivars with greater uptake and translocation accumulate more.

Published work points in the same direction. Sonu et al. (2025) found genotype governs grain micronutrient concentration, Kumar et al. (2022) reported trace metals shift between bran and endosperm rather than being lost. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed soluble minerals move inward from husk and pericarp, Hu et al. (2019) recorded water moving inside the kernel displaces elements from the aleurone. The most favourable entry differed between products. Dudeshwar, Harinakhuri and Radhatilak each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional disorder in rice eating populations, so the iron retained in the product is of direct importance. A higher content is better. For table rice the values lay between 2.24 and 9.94 ppm, with the control at 2.24 ppm. 9 cultivars exceeded the control and Kalojira ranked first. In khichdi the values ranged from 1.51 in Lal Badshabhog to 2.23 ppm in Kalojira. The control recorded 2.02 ppm, 2 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalojira gave the most favourable value. Kalojira recorded the highest value in pulao at 1.43 ppm and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.89 ppm. Against 1.13 ppm for the control, 2 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalojira was the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 1.50 and 5.03 ppm, with the control at 3.92 ppm. Here one cultivar exceeded the control and Kalonunia ranked highest. Table 4.51 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.16. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. In 4 products the year effect was significant and in 4 the year by cultivar interaction, so the cultivars kept similar order in both years. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 1.27 to 3.51%.

Grain iron depends on the amount remobilised from the flag leaf and on the chelators that transport it, both of which differ between cultivars. Cooking moves some of it inward from the pericarp. The same pattern has been reported before. Sonu et al. (2025) showed grain iron is heritable but few lines reach nutritional targets, Kumar et al. (2022) noted iron moves inward and becomes more available. Jannasch and Wang (2020) concluded the steep water can carry iron and calcium into the endosperm, Akter et al. (2025) demonstrated iron fell while protein and zinc were concentrated.
The leading cultivar changed with the product, Kalojira and Kalonunia ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Zinc is required for immunity, growth and wound healing, and is the mineral after iron most often deficient in rice based diets. A higher content is better. In table rice the values ranged from 0.43 in Harinakhuri to 0.58 ppm in Tulaipanji. The control recorded 0.52 ppm, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Tulaipanji gave the most favourable value. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in khichdi at 1.06 ppm and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.36 ppm. Against 0.57 ppm for the control, 5 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhatilak was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 0.25 and 0.43 ppm, with the control at 0.25 ppm. Here 8 cultivars exceeded the control, with Kalojira the highest. In payash the values ranged from 0.37 in Radhunipagal to 0.83 ppm in Kalonunia. The control recorded 0.77 ppm, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalonunia gave the most favourable value. The data are presented in Table 4.52 and plotted in Fig. 4.17.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. The year term was significant in 4 products and the year by cultivar term in 1, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. Coefficients of variation lay between 4.97 and 6.33%, so the trial was precise. Zinc loading depends on the HMA2 and HMA4 transporters and on remobilisation during grain filling. It is held in the aleurone largely as phytate salts.

Earlier reports support this finding. Kumar et al. (2022) found zinc moves outward on treatment, unlike iron, Sonu et al. (2025) reported grain zinc is polygenic with wide genotypic variance. Hu et al. (2019) observed zinc is held in the germ and aleurone, Oliveira et al. (2026) recorded polishing matters more than the thermal step. The leading position was shared between Kalojira, Kalonunia, Radhatilak and Tulaipanji, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Manganese is required by superoxide dismutase and certain other enzymes. The dietary requirement is small but cereals supply most of it, so a higher content is better. Kataribhog recorded the highest value in table rice at 0.86 ppm and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.45 ppm. Against 0.45 ppm for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kataribhog was the most favourable entry. For khichdi the values lay between 0.22 and 0.58 ppm, with the control at 0.30 ppm. Radhatilak ranked first, and 7 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In pulao the values ranged from 0.09 in Harinakhuri to 0.41 ppm in Kataribhog. The control recorded 0.24 ppm, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kataribhog gave the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in payash at 0.38 ppm and Radhunipagal the lowest at 0.17 ppm. Against 0.38 ppm for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. Table 4.53 lists the means and Fig. 4.18 presents them graphically. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. Year mattered in 4 products and the year by cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. The coefficient of variation ran from 4.14 to 5.82%, which points to reliable measurement.

Manganese enters through NRAMP and MTP transporters and accumulates in the aleurone, so the value depends on uptake and on how much of the outer grain survives milling. Similar results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) showed aleurone bound elements are displaced as water redistributes, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted soluble minerals migrate inward during steeping. Sonu et al. (2025) concluded genotype counts for more than environment in mineral density, Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated retention depends on the starting level and the treatment.
Dudeshwar, Kataribhog and Radhatilak each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Lightness measures how pale the product has remained. It falls with browning and with inward movement of pigments, so a higher value generally indicates gentler processing. For table rice the values lay between 66.67 and 73.59, with the control at 72.74. Here one cultivar exceeded the control and Lal Badshabhog ranked highest. In khichdi the values ranged from 50.72 in Lal Badshabhog to 61.85 in Dudeshwar. The control recorded 61.85, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value. Kalojira recorded the highest value in pulao at 70.05 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 54.60. The control gave 54.60; 9 cultivars exceeded it, Kalojira most markedly. For payash the values lay between 72.42 and 78.21, with the control at 77.63. 2 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Radhatilak ranked highest. The means are given in Table 4.54 and plotted in Fig. 4.19.

The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. Significance attached to year in 2 products and to the year by cultivar interaction in 3, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 0.20 and 0.49%. Lightness falls as browning products accumulate and as pericarp pigments dissolve and migrate inward. Cultivars with more reducing sugar and free amino nitrogen brown further under the same treatment.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found darkening comes from pigment movement and browning, Srisang et al. (2021) reported lightness falls as the thermal treatment becomes harsher. Panda et al. (2021) observed shorter heating gives a lighter product at the same moisture loss, Akter et al. (2025) recorded a darker product was still preferred overall. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Dudeshwar, Kalojira, Lal Badshabhog and Radhatilak ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

The a* value is signed: a positive value places the sample on the red side of the green to red axis and a negative value on the green side. Redness increases as browning proceeds, so a lower value is preferred. In table rice the values ranged from -5.09 in Lal Badshabhog to -3.05 in Kalojira. The control recorded -4.69, one cultivar exceeded the control, and Lal Badshabhog gave the most favourable value. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in khichdi at 5.32 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 1.27. Against 1.27 for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between -6.33 and 2.24, with the control at -6.33.
