Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In payash the values ranged from -5.70 in Dudeshwar to -4.38 in Kalonunia. The control recorded -5.70, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value. Table 4.55 gives the means and Fig. 4.20 shows them. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. In 2 products the year effect was significant and in 1 the year by cultivar interaction, so the cultivars kept similar order in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from -2.39 to 2.93%, indicating good experimental precision.

Redness rises as melanoidins and their coloured precursors accumulate, and the rate depends on the reducing sugars and free amino acids the cultivar supplies. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed the amber shift comes from Maillard browning, Srisang et al. (2021) noted colour builds with time and temperature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) concluded how far colour develops is cultivar specific, Panda et al. (2021) demonstrated shorter heating limits colour development.
The most favourable entry differed between products. Dudeshwar and Lal Badshabhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Yellowness arises from bran pigments migrating into the endosperm and from early browning products. Except where a golden colour is required, a lower value is better. Lal Badshabhog recorded the highest value in table rice at 111.41 and Radhunipagal the lowest at 103.18. Relative to 110.01 for the control, 8 cultivars were higher, with Radhunipagal the best among them. For khichdi the values lay between 81.65 and 97.61, with the control at 97.61. 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Lal Badshabhog being the highest among them. In pulao the values ranged from 86.09 in Dudeshwar to 107.22 in Kalojira. The control recorded 86.09, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value. Lal Badshabhog recorded the highest value in payash at 117.27 and Kataribhog the lowest at 110.38. The control recorded 116.43. 7 cultivars exceeded it and Kataribhog ranked most favourable. The values appear in Table 4.56, with Fig. 4.21 showing the same data.

Significance was reached in each of the products. The year term was significant in 2 products and the year by cultivar term in 1, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. With coefficients of variation of 0.20 to 0.34%, the experiment was well controlled. Yellowness arises from carotenoids and flavonoids carried in from the pericarp during hydration together with early browning products, so cultivars with more pigment give higher values.

This agrees with what has been reported before. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found bran pigments dissolve on soaking and fix on drying, Srisang et al. (2021) reported yellowing is proportional to the heat load. Devi and Badwaik (2022) observed colour readings track pigment composition, Oliveira et al. (2026) recorded final colour depends on pigment and on processing together. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Dudeshwar, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

This measures the overall colour distance between the product and the raw grain. A smaller value means the grain has changed in texture without changing greatly in appearance. For table rice the values lay between 32.27 and 40.74, with the control at 39.26. 8 cultivars exceeded the control and Radhunipagal ranked first. In khichdi the values ranged from 26.96 in Lal Badshabhog to 30.98 in Dudeshwar. With the control at 30.98, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Lal Badshabhog was the best. Kalojira recorded the highest value in pulao at 16.25 and Gobindabhog the lowest at 0.18. Against 13.44 for the control, 7 cultivars exceeded it, and Gobindabhog was the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 39.10 and 47.01, with the control at 46.00. Here 6 cultivars exceeded the control, with Kataribhog the highest. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.57 and illustrated in Fig. 4.22. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. Year mattered in 2 products and the year by cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. The coefficient of variation stayed within 0.57 to 2.80%, a sign of good precision.

This combines all three colour coordinates and so registers both pigment migration and browning, each of which scales with what the cultivar provides. Earlier work points the same way. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed colour is the main barrier to accepting processed rice, Srisang et al. (2021) noted a combined colour index separates treatments better than one axis. Panda et al. (2021) concluded the same processing can be had at a smaller colour cost, Akter et al. (2025) demonstrated overall colour change matched what the panel judged.
The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Radhunipagal, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Spreading in dilute alkali is inversely related to gelatinisation temperature. A higher spreading value means the grain gelatinises at a lower temperature and so cooks in less time and with less fuel. In table rice the values ranged from 3.01 in Dudeshwar to 4.81 in Kalonunia. The control recorded 3.01, 9 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalonunia was the most favourable. Table 4.58 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.23.

The analysis of variance gave F = 5601.84 for cultivars, a critical difference of 0.04 and a coefficient of variation of 0.50%. Disintegration in alkali depends on the crystalline order of the starch granule, which is governed by amylopectin chain length under starch synthase IIa, so the ranking follows gelatinisation temperature.

Published work points in the same direction. Little et al. (1958) found the alkali test became the routine measure of gelatinisation, Bocevska et al. (2009) reported the spreading score matches instrumental gelatinisation. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) observed cultivars of different gelatinisation temperature respond differently, Armstrong et al. (2022) recorded the spreading value can be predicted by near infrared. Kalonunia gave the most favourable value here, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Elongation on cooking is the property for which the fine and aromatic grades are valued, since it gives the long slender cooked grain. A higher ratio is better. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in table rice at 1.77 and Kalonunia the lowest at 1.40. The control gave 1.71; 2 cultivars exceeded it, Radhunipagal most markedly. The data are presented in Table 4.59 and plotted in Fig. 4.24. The analysis of variance gave F = 329.88 for cultivars, a critical difference of 0.04 and a coefficient of variation of 1.15%.

Elongation depends on the axial arrangement of the endosperm cells and on amylose restraining radial swelling, both under cultivar control. The same pattern has been reported before. Buggenhout et al. (2013) showed cultivar is the main determinant of kernel behaviour, Buggenhout et al. (2014) noted kernel strength governs the response to stress. Cheng et al. (2019) concluded expansion follows gelatinisation and setting back, Devi and Badwaik (2022) demonstrated traditional cultivars differ widely in cooking behaviour.
Radhunipagal gave the most favourable value here, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Volume expansion determines the cooked yield from a given weight of raw grain, and in the puffed and popped forms it produces the light open texture. A higher ratio is better. For table rice the values lay between 2.00 and 4.85, with the control at 4.85. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. Table 4.60 lists the means and Fig. 4.25 presents them graphically.

The analysis of variance gave F = 11006.68 for cultivars, a critical difference of 0.04 and a coefficient of variation of 0.62%. Expansion depends on the degree of starch gelatinisation and on the mechanical resistance of the endosperm, so a compact endosperm with sufficient amylose expands furthest without fissuring.

Earlier reports support this finding. Cheng et al. (2019) found swelling is limited by how far the starch gelatinises, Buggenhout et al. (2014) reported kernel strength decides whether expansion holds or the grain cracks. Tian et al. (2018) observed lower crystallinity changes swelling, Devi and Badwaik (2022) recorded expansion and water uptake follow amylose content. Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value here, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Aroma distinguishes the traditional aromatic cultivars from ordinary grain and arises mainly from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. A higher score is clearly better. In table rice the values ranged from 4.94 in Dudeshwar to 8.48 in Kalojira. Against the control at 4.94, 9 cultivars ranked higher, Kalojira being the highest. Kalojira recorded the highest value in khichdi at 8.42 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.35. Relative to 6.35 for the control, 8 cultivars were higher, with Kalojira the best among them. For pulao the values lay between 5.12 and 8.88, with the control at 5.12. Radhunipagal ranked first, and 9 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In payash the values ranged from 4.87 in Dudeshwar to 8.19 in Gobindabhog. The control gave 4.87; 9 cultivars exceeded that value and Gobindabhog ranked first. The means are given in Table 4.61 and plotted in Fig. 4.26. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. Significance attached to year in 1 products and to the year by cultivar interaction in 1, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 3.47 to 4.29%.

Aroma arises mainly from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, which accumulates when the BADH2 gene is non functional and its precursor is free to cyclise. The compound is volatile, so thermal exposure also matters. Similar results have been published elsewhere. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) showed sensory character shifts with treatment in a cultivar specific way, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted over processing gives off odours through lipid oxidation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) concluded aroma is one of the attributes traditional products are graded on, Panda et al. (2021) demonstrated shorter heating keeps more of the volatiles.
The leading cultivar changed with the product, Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Flavour combines aroma, taste and mouthfeel, and is among the strongest determinants of whether a product is accepted or rejected. Kataribhog recorded the highest value in table rice at 8.26 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 5.79. The control recorded 5.79. 9 cultivars exceeded it and Kataribhog ranked most favourable. For khichdi the values lay between 5.43 and 8.81, with the control at 5.43. 9 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Lal Badshabhog ranked highest. In pulao the values ranged from 6.59 in Dudeshwar to 8.86 in Kataribhog. With the control at 6.59, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Kataribhog was the best. Tulaipanji recorded the highest value in payash at 8.18 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.05. Against 6.05 for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded it, and Tulaipanji was the most favourable entry. Table 4.62 gives the means and Fig. 4.27 shows them.

Significance was reached in each of the products. The year effect was not significant in any product, though the year by cultivar interaction was significant in 1, so in that product the difference between cultivars was not of the same magnitude in both years. Coefficients of variation lay between 2.05 and 3.88%, so the trial was precise. Flavour combines the volatile fraction with the sugars and amino acids released on cooking and with the texture of the grain, so cultivars strong in aroma and moderate in firmness score well.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) found flavour responds to processing more sensitively than instruments do, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported flavour improves with firmer texture until treatment goes too far. Roy et al. (2019) observed flavour moves with the bioactive and physicochemical properties, Akter et al. (2025) recorded flavour and texture outweighed colour in overall liking. The leading position was shared between Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Tulaipanji, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Appearance governs the first impression and therefore whether the product is tried at all. For table rice the values lay between 6.95 and 8.43, with the control at 6.95. 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhatilak being the highest among them. In khichdi the values ranged from 5.80 in Radhatilak to 8.54 in Kalonunia. The control recorded 7.05, 5 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalonunia was the most favourable. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in pulao at 8.72 and Kataribhog the lowest at 5.96. Against 8.05 for the control, one cultivar exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal was the most favourable entry. For payash the values lay between 6.58 and 8.58, with the control at 6.58. 6 cultivars exceeded the control and Gobindabhog ranked first. The values appear in Table 4.63, with Fig. 4.28 showing the same data. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. No significance attached to year or to its interaction with cultivar, and the order stood in both seasons. The coefficient of variation ran from 1.39 to 4.08%, which points to reliable measurement.

Appearance follows the colour coordinates, which are determined by pigment migration and browning, so the cultivars that remain pale head the ranking. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed colour is among the two attributes that most limit acceptance, Dutta and Mahanta (2014) noted appearance caps the market whatever the nutritional merit. Srisang et al. (2021) concluded harder processing gives a visibly darker product, Akter et al. (2025) demonstrated a darker product was nonetheless more acceptable overall.
Gobindabhog, Kalonunia, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Consistency describes the textural coherence of the finished dish and how well it matches what the preparation requires. In table rice the values ranged from 7.43 in Lal Badshabhog to 8.35 in Radhatilak. Against the control at 7.72, 4 cultivars ranked higher, Radhatilak being the highest. Kalojira recorded the highest value in khichdi at 8.51 and Gobindabhog the lowest at 6.88. The control gave 7.02; 6 cultivars exceeded it, Kalojira most markedly. For pulao the values lay between 6.83 and 8.01, with the control at 7.93. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked highest. In payash the values ranged from 6.78 in Kalonunia to 8.41 in Gobindabhog. The control gave 7.13; 2 cultivars exceeded that value and Gobindabhog ranked first. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.64 and illustrated in Fig. 4.29.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Year had no significant effect, alone or in combination with cultivar, so the ranking repeated. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 1.44 and 4.51%. Consistency depends on the degree of starch gelatinisation and subsequent retrogradation, and on the protein network surrounding the granules.

Published work agrees. Cheng et al. (2019) found heat and moisture give a firmer, less sticky network, Iqbal et al. (2021) reported firmness follows the starch and protein network. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed texture and colour together decide acceptance, Devi and Badwaik (2022) recorded texture and pasting follow amylose and starch structure. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Gobindabhog, Harinakhuri, Kalojira and Radhatilak ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Cooking quality summarises water uptake, cooking time and the structural integrity of the cooked grain. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in table rice at 8.42 and Lal Badshabhog the lowest at 7.36. Relative to 7.70 for the control, 5 cultivars were higher, with Radhatilak the best among them. For khichdi the values lay between 7.00 and 8.45, with the control at 7.07. Here 7 cultivars exceeded the control, with Lal Badshabhog the highest. In pulao the values ranged from 5.85 in Lal Badshabhog to 8.28 in Radhunipagal. With the control at 7.08, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Radhunipagal was the best. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in payash at 8.18 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.80. The control recorded 6.80. 8 cultivars exceeded it and Gobindabhog ranked most favourable. Table 4.65 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.30. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. Year and its interaction with cultivar both fell short of significance, so the order was the same in each year. With coefficients of variation of 1.49 to 3.86%, the experiment was well controlled.

Cooking quality depends on gelatinisation temperature, amylose content and the structural integrity of the grain, which is why it tracks alkali spreading value and amylose. Previous reports run along the same lines. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) showed cooking behaviour changes steadily with treatment severity, Kwofie and Ngadi (2017) noted time and temperature are the processor's main control. Buggenhout et al. (2013) concluded cultivar and processing history act together, Cheng et al. (2019) demonstrated gelatinisation governs water uptake and cooking time.

The most favourable entry differed between products. Gobindabhog, Lal Badshabhog, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

The analysis of variance answers one attribute at a time, so a single figure was needed to establish which cultivar is best overall. This was done using the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), where each attribute is scored, weighted for its importance, and the weighted scores summed. Kraggerud et al. (2012) later examined whether such a score genuinely reflects overall quality and concluded that it does. Here every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was put on a scale of 0 to 100, oriented so that 100 always denotes the better outcome, then averaged within five groups and combined by weight: sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. The weights are a stated convention rather than a property of the data, and the index may be recomputed under any alternative set. The result is given in Table 4.66, and the score of every cultivar in every group appears in Table 4.68.

On this index the best cultivar was Kalojira for table rice; Radhunipagal for khichdi; Kataribhog for pulao; Gobindabhog for payash. The control came at or near the bottom in every product, so replacing Dudeshwar with the cultivars named here would improve the product without any change in the method of preparation. Table 4.67 gives, for each product, the cultivar with the best balance of attributes against the control.

The table below gives the five group scores and the composite score for every cultivar in every product, so the standing of any entry may be read directly. The weights applied were sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.

sec: 4.19 Verification of the weights using principal component analysis (Part A)
text: The weights above were chosen rather than calculated, so the ranking was checked against a second set of weights taken from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was run on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading times the share of variance that component carries. Such is the usual way of setting weights for a composite indicator without judgement. The two rankings agreed closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.942 and a lowest value of 0.867, and the same cultivar came first in 3 of the 4 products, as Table 4.69 shows. The ranking therefore follows from the data and not from the particular weights chosen. Principal component analysis is used here only to set the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, because a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the better one.

sec: 4.19 Verification of the weights using principal component analysis (Part A)
text: The mean rank correlation was 0.942 and the lowest 0.867, and the same cultivar came first in 3 of the 4 products. The ranking is therefore not an artefact of the weights chosen. Where the two disagreed, the cultivars concerned were close together on the index in any case, so the disagreement is one of order between near equals rather than of substance.

Cluster analysis was used to examine how the cultivars and the products group together when all the attributes are considered simultaneously. The 40 cultivar and product combinations were standardised on the 22 attributes measured in every product, and Ward's method was applied to the Euclidean distances between them. The number of groups was set at 4. Where a cluster contains only one product, it is the method of preparation that determines the quality profile; where cultivars of different products fall together, the two are comparable in the finished form.

Of the 4 clusters, 3 contain only one product. This indicates that the products differ from one another more than the cultivars differ within any one product. Amarnath and Ravi Kumar (2025) used Ward's method in the same way in rice and drew on the cluster means to pick genotypes for further work, on the reasoning that crosses between distant clusters are more likely to give useful variation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) made the same point from the product side, that different traditional preparations need genuinely different raw material.

Nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal were tested against Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar used as the control, in the 4 cooked products of this group. Each was grown and prepared in the same way for two years and analysed as a pooled completely randomised design. In every product the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes measured, while the year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for far fewer. The main finding is therefore straightforward: the choice of cultivar determines the quality of the product, and the year of production makes much less difference. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally hold its position in the next.

On this index the best cultivar was Kalojira for table rice; Radhunipagal for khichdi; Kataribhog for pulao; Gobindabhog for payash. The control came at or near the bottom in every product, so replacing Dudeshwar with the cultivars named here would improve the product without any change in the method of preparation. Table 4.67 gives, for each product, the cultivar with the best balance of attributes against the control.

The weights above were chosen rather than calculated, so the ranking was checked against a second set of weights taken from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was run on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading times the share of variance that component carries. This is the common way of setting weights for a composite indicator without judgement. The two rankings agreed closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.942 and a lowest value of 0.867, and the same cultivar came first in 3 of the 4 products, as Table 4.69 shows. The ranking therefore follows from the data and not from the particular weights chosen. Principal component analysis is used here only to set the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, because a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the better one.

Cluster analysis was then run on all 40 cultivar and product combinations together, using the 22 attributes measured in every product. Ward's method placed them in 4 groups, of which 3 contained a single product only (Table 4.70 and Fig. 4.31). When the products are compared with one another, therefore, it is the method of preparation rather than the cultivar that determines the broad quality type, whereas within any one product the cultivar is the variable under the control of the processor. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory: the preparation determines the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.

The cultivars named here should be tested again on a larger scale and over more years before being recommended generally. For breeding work aimed at improving the group as a whole, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are more likely to release useful variation.

Amylose content determines the firmness and separateness of the cooked grain. A higher content gives a firmer, drier grain that holds its shape, and a lower content a softer, stickier one. In popped rice the values ranged from 15.66 in Harinakhuri to 19.64% in Kalojira. The control recorded 16.97%, 8 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalojira was the most favourable. Kalojira recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 19.69% and Harinakhuri the lowest at 15.64%. Against 17.38% for the control, 7 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalojira was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 16.00 and 20.01%, with the control at 17.61%. Kalonunia ranked first, and 8 cultivars in all exceeded the control. The data are presented in Table 4.71 and plotted in Fig. 4.32.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. In 1 products the year effect was significant and in 1 the year by cultivar interaction, so the cultivars kept similar order in both years. The coefficient of variation stayed within 0.10 to 0.89%, a sign of good precision. Amylose is laid down by granule bound starch synthase I at the Waxy locus, and cultivars differ in the allele they carry. Cooking disorganises the granule but does not alter the amount of amylose present.

Published work agrees. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found apparent amylose decides eating and processing behaviour, Tian et al. (2018) reported crystallinity and digestibility fall without amylose changing. Cheng et al. (2019) observed heat and moisture rebuild the matrix into a firmer gel, Devi and Badwaik (2022) recorded amylose explains most of the varietal difference in cooking. The most favourable entry differed between products. Kalojira and Kalonunia each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Starch is the energy supplying fraction of the grain and the basis of its texture. A higher value indicates a well filled endosperm and good recovery of the edible fraction. Harinakhuri recorded the highest value in popped rice at 77.07% and Kataribhog the lowest at 73.00%. The control gave 73.11%; 8 cultivars exceeded it, Harinakhuri most markedly. For puffed rice the values lay between 73.85 and 78.50%, with the control at 75.41%. Here one cultivar exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 70.22 in Dudeshwar to 74.15% in Harinakhuri. Against the control at 70.22%, 8 cultivars ranked higher, Harinakhuri being the highest. Table 4.72 lists the means and Fig. 4.33 presents them graphically. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. Neither year nor the year by cultivar term reached significance; ranking was unchanged between years. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 0.31 to 1.41%.

Starch content depends on how efficiently assimilate was moved into the endosperm during grain filling. In the prepared product it is further affected by the loss of low molecular weight material and by the water taken up in cooking. Previous reports run along the same lines. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed starch makes up about nine tenths of milled rice by dry weight, Tian et al. (2018) noted the residual starch is swollen and less crystalline. Iqbal et al. (2021) concluded restructured starch resists digestion, Cheng et al. (2019) demonstrated how far the starch gelatinises drives texture and digestion.
Harinakhuri gave the most favourable value in every product of this group, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Protein is the main nutritional contribution of rice after energy, and it also firms the cooked grain through disulphide bonding. For popped rice the values lay between 6.57 and 7.63%, with the control at 6.68%. 4 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Radhunipagal ranked highest. In puffed rice the values ranged from 6.23 in Harinakhuri to 7.15% in Gobindabhog. The control gave 6.54%; 2 cultivars exceeded that value and Gobindabhog ranked first. Kalojira recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 7.23% and Radhatilak the lowest at 6.13%. Against 6.52% for the control, one cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalojira was the most favourable entry. The means are given in Table 4.73 and plotted in Fig. 4.34.

The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. No significance attached to year or to its interaction with cultivar, and the order stood in both seasons. Coefficients of variation lay between 2.46 and 4.36%, so the trial was precise. Most of the protein is glutelin stored in protein bodies beneath the aleurone, and the amount depends on the nitrogen moved into the grain during filling. Cooking does not alter it.

Published work points in the same direction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found total protein is unchanged by hydrothermal treatment. Cheng et al. (2019) reported disulphide cross links raise firmness, and Akter et al. (2025) observed protein rose from 6.68 to 9.42% after treatment; Iqbal et al. (2021) found the protein network controls enzyme access to starch. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Soluble protein is the fraction that remains extractable, and therefore digestible, after cooking. A higher value indicates that heat has not aggregated the protein. In popped rice the values ranged from 0.47 in Dudeshwar to 0.60% in Kataribhog. With the control at 0.47%, 5 cultivars exceeded it and Kataribhog was the best. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 1.97% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 1.21%. Relative to 1.21% for the control, 9 cultivars were higher, with Radhunipagal the best among them. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.93 and 1.39%, with the control at 1.06%. 7 cultivars exceeded the control, Kalojira being the highest among them. Table 4.74 gives the means and Fig. 4.35 shows them. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. Year had no significant effect, alone or in combination with cultivar, so the ranking repeated. The coefficient of variation ran from 1.17 to 3.48%, which points to reliable measurement.

Heat ruptures the protein bodies and then cross links the released chains through disulphide bonds, which lowers the extractable fraction. Cultivars richer in cysteine lose more. The same pattern has been reported before. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded solubility changes while total protein does not, Cheng et al. (2019) showed cross linking lowers the extractable fraction. Kabir et al. (2025) noted treatment changes how protein and bound phenolics associate, Roy et al. (2019) concluded solubility falls as steam and soaking become more severe.
Kalojira, Kataribhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Lipid is located in the germ and aleurone and carries the fat soluble vitamins and the aroma compounds. A higher content is better, although excess lipid shortens shelf life. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in popped rice at 1.97% and Tulaipanji the lowest at 1.66%. Against 1.79% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalonunia was the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 0.68 and 0.93%, with the control at 0.75%. Here one cultivar exceeded the control and Kalojira ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 1.33 in Gobindabhog to 1.53% in Tulaipanji. The control recorded 1.43%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Tulaipanji gave the most favourable value. The values appear in Table 4.75, with Fig. 4.36 showing the same data.

The cultivar effect was significant in 1 products out of 3. The year effect was significant in 1 product, but the interaction was not significant anywhere, so the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 7.81 and 9.86%. Lipid is stored as triacylglycerol in the germ and aleurone, so the value reflects both the size of these tissues in the cultivar and the extent of milling.

Earlier reports support this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated lipid sits in germ and aleurone and oxidises readily, Hu et al. (2019) found moving water inside the kernel shifts the lipid bearing tissues. Devi and Badwaik (2022) reported traditional cultivars differ widely in proximate composition, Oliveira et al. (2026) observed milling is the main route by which the outer layers are lost. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Kalojira, Kalonunia and Tulaipanji ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Ash is the residue remaining after ignition and represents the total inorganic contribution of the grain. For popped rice the values lay between 1.33 and 1.74%, with the control at 1.60%. 2 cultivars exceeded the control and Lal Badshabhog ranked first. In puffed rice the values ranged from 0.26 in Kataribhog to 0.72% in Dudeshwar. The control recorded 0.72%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 1.48% and Kataribhog the lowest at 1.09%. Against 1.48% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.76 and illustrated in Fig. 4.37. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. The year effect was not significant in any product, though the year by cultivar interaction was significant in 1, so in that product the difference between cultivars was not of the same magnitude in both years. With coefficients of variation of 1.24 to 3.17%, the experiment was well controlled.

Ash follows the germ and aleurone, which carry most of the mineral matter, so cultivars with a thicker aleurone or a larger embryo give higher values. Similar results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) recorded ash follows how much germ and aleurone survive, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed the spread in ash comes from the outer grain layers. Jannasch and Wang (2020) noted the steeping medium can add to the mineral fraction, Kumar et al. (2022) concluded ash is redistributed rather than lost on treatment.
The most favourable entry differed between products. Dudeshwar and Lal Badshabhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Bagchi et al. (2021) compared popped, beaten, puffed and boiled products of four black rice cultivars and a white reference and found popped rice to rank first for phenolic compounds, vitamin E, gamma-oryzanol and antioxidant activity, with boiled rice the poorest. The higher bioactive scores of the popped product in the present study, and the low position of boiled table rice in Part A, agree with that ranking.

Phenolic acids are the principal antioxidants of the grain and are largely bound to the pericarp cell wall. A higher retained content in the product is better. In popped rice the values ranged from 3.50 in Harinakhuri to 5.53 mg GAE/g in Tulaipanji. The control recorded 3.89 mg GAE/g, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Tulaipanji gave the most favourable value. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 13.74 mg GAE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.42 mg GAE/g. Against 6.42 mg GAE/g for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhatilak was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 2.05 and 4.36 mg GAE/g, with the control at 2.54 mg GAE/g. Here 8 cultivars exceeded the control, with Gobindabhog the highest. Table 4.77 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.38.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. The year term was significant in 3 products and the year by cultivar term in 3, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. The coefficient of variation stayed within 1.22 to 2.30%, a sign of good precision. Most phenolic acid is bound to arabinoxylan in the pericarp wall. Heat cleaves these bonds and releases it, while simultaneously degrading and leaching the free fraction, so the value recorded is the balance of the two.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Phimphilai et al. (2026) demonstrated popping and steam cooking cut total phenolics sharply, Shavandi et al. (2023) found infrared puffing raises the extractable fraction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported heat frees ferulic and p-coumaric acid from the cell wall, Kabir et al. (2025) observed soaking and cooking lower phenolic acids, bound exceeding free. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Gobindabhog, Radhatilak and Tulaipanji ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Flavonoids contribute to antioxidant activity and to pericarp colour. They degrade readily on heating, so the residual content indicates how gently the grain was treated. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.52 mg QE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.23 mg QE/g. Against 0.23 mg QE/g for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhatilak was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.03 and 0.41 mg QE/g, with the control at 0.03 mg QE/g. Gobindabhog ranked first, and 8 cultivars in all exceeded the control. The data are presented in Table 4.78 and plotted in Fig. 4.39. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. Year mattered in 2 products and the year by cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 4.16 to 8.36%.

Flavonoids are synthesised in the pericarp and cultivars differ in the amount deposited. They are readily destroyed by heat, so the residual content reflects both the initial level and the treatment. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Phimphilai et al. (2026) recorded flavonoids break down more readily than total phenolics, Kabir et al. (2025) showed most flavonoid sits in the bound fraction. Oliveira et al. (2026) noted long cooking can cost up to forty per cent, Devi and Badwaik (2022) concluded traditional cultivars differ several fold.
The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog and Radhatilak, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Antioxidant capacity measures the activity of the whole bioactive fraction rather than its quantity, so a higher value is desirable. For popped rice the values lay between 9.67 and 12.64 mg TE/g, with the control at 9.67 mg TE/g. 9 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Kalonunia ranked highest. In puffed rice the values ranged from 1.46 in Dudeshwar to 4.19 mg TE/g in Radhunipagal. The control recorded 1.46 mg TE/g, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal gave the most favourable value. Kataribhog recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 3.14 mg TE/g and Kalonunia the lowest at 1.57 mg TE/g. Against 2.50 mg TE/g for the control, 6 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kataribhog was the most favourable entry. Table 4.79 lists the means and Fig. 4.40 presents them graphically.

The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. The year effect was significant in 3 products, but the interaction was not significant anywhere, so the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.51 and 1.80%, so the trial was precise. Antioxidant capacity derives from the surviving phenolics and flavonoids together with browning products formed during heating, so cultivars rich in bound phenolics retain more of it.

This agrees with what has been reported before. Phimphilai et al. (2026) demonstrated capacity tracks phenolic and flavonoid content, Shavandi et al. (2023) found activity moves with total phenolics as puffing changes. Kabir et al. (2025) reported the bound phenolics account for most of the activity, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed browning products add to measured activity. Kalonunia, Kataribhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Phytic acid binds iron, zinc and calcium in the intestine and prevents their absorption. A lower content is therefore better, since it releases the very minerals the grain supplies. In popped rice the values ranged from 0.12 in Kalonunia to 0.32% in Kataribhog. The control recorded 0.26%, 6 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalonunia was the most favourable. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.44% and Kalojira the lowest at 0.20%. Against 0.21% for the control, one cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalojira was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.20 and 0.47%, with the control at 0.37%. 5 cultivars exceeded the control, Tulaipanji being the highest among them. The means are given in Table 4.80 and plotted in Fig. 4.41. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. Significance attached to year in 1 products and to the year by cultivar interaction in 1, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. The coefficient of variation ran from 2.46 to 6.95%, which points to reliable measurement.

Phytate is deposited as globoids in the aleurone during grain filling and is hydrolysed by endogenous phytase during soaking, so the residue depends on both processes. Earlier work points the same way. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded treated brown rice holds about half the phytate of untreated, Kumar et al. (2022) showed less phytate means more iron and zinc absorbed. Bhar et al. (2022) noted cutting phytate is a main nutritional argument for processed grain, Hu et al. (2019) concluded germination and hydrothermal treatment work in different ways.
No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Kalojira, Kalonunia and Tulaipanji ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Copper is required for iron transport and for several enzymes, and cereals are a principal dietary source. A higher content in the product is better. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in popped rice at 0.51 ppm and Radhatilak the lowest at 0.38 ppm. Against 0.51 ppm for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 0.29 and 0.62 ppm, with the control at 0.42 ppm. 2 cultivars exceeded the control and Kataribhog ranked first. In flattened rice the values ranged from 0.33 in Radhunipagal to 0.55 ppm in Lal Badshabhog. The control recorded 0.52 ppm, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Lal Badshabhog gave the most favourable value. Table 4.81 gives the means and Fig. 4.42 shows them.

Significance was reached in each of the products. In 3 products the year effect was significant and in 2 the year by cultivar interaction, so the cultivars kept similar order in both years. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 6.04 and 6.11%. Copper is carried into the grain by COPT and HMA transporters and stored mainly in the aleurone, so cultivars with greater uptake and translocation accumulate more.

Published work points in the same direction. Sonu et al. (2025) demonstrated genotype governs grain micronutrient concentration, Kumar et al. (2022) found trace metals shift between bran and endosperm rather than being lost. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported soluble minerals move inward from husk and pericarp, Hu et al. (2019) observed water moving inside the kernel displaces elements from the aleurone. The most favourable entry differed between products. Dudeshwar, Kataribhog and Lal Badshabhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional disorder in rice eating populations, so the iron retained in the product is of direct importance. A higher content is better. For popped rice the values lay between 2.77 and 3.70 ppm, with the control at 3.10 ppm. Here 4 cultivars exceeded the control, with Gobindabhog the highest. In puffed rice the values ranged from 0.93 in Radhunipagal to 1.76 ppm in Harinakhuri. The control recorded 1.31 ppm, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Harinakhuri gave the most favourable value. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 3.75 ppm and Tulaipanji the lowest at 1.83 ppm. Against 2.59 ppm for the control, 3 cultivars exceeded the control, and Gobindabhog was the most favourable entry. The values appear in Table 4.82, with Fig. 4.43 showing the same data. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. The year term was significant in 3 products and the year by cultivar term in 3, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. With coefficients of variation of 1.80 to 3.52%, the experiment was well controlled.

Grain iron depends on the amount remobilised from the flag leaf and on the chelators that transport it, both of which differ between cultivars. Cooking moves some of it inward from the pericarp. The same pattern has been reported before. Sonu et al. (2025) recorded grain iron is heritable but few lines reach nutritional targets, Kumar et al. (2022) showed iron moves inward and becomes more available. Jannasch and Wang (2020) noted the steep water can carry iron and calcium into the endosperm, Akter et al. (2025) concluded iron fell while protein and zinc were concentrated.
The leading cultivar changed with the product, Gobindabhog and Harinakhuri ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Zinc is required for immunity, growth and wound healing, and is the mineral after iron most often deficient in rice based diets. A higher content is better. In popped rice the values ranged from 0.60 in Dudeshwar to 0.79 ppm in Kataribhog. The control recorded 0.60 ppm, 6 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kataribhog gave the most favourable value. Kalojira recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.42 ppm and Lal Badshabhog the lowest at 0.21 ppm. Against 0.33 ppm for the control, 5 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalojira was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.48 and 1.36 ppm, with the control at 0.57 ppm. Gobindabhog ranked first, and 2 cultivars in all exceeded the control. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.83 and illustrated in Fig. 4.44.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Year mattered in 3 products and the year by cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. The coefficient of variation stayed within 5.21 to 6.38%, a sign of good precision. Zinc loading depends on the HMA2 and HMA4 transporters and on remobilisation during grain filling. It is held in the aleurone largely as phytate salts.

Earlier reports support this finding. Kumar et al. (2022) demonstrated zinc moves outward on treatment, unlike iron, Sonu et al. (2025) found grain zinc is polygenic with wide genotypic variance. Hu et al. (2019) reported zinc is held in the germ and aleurone, Oliveira et al. (2026) observed polishing matters more than the thermal step. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Kataribhog, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Manganese is required by superoxide dismutase and certain other enzymes. The dietary requirement is small but cereals supply most of it, so a higher content is better. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in popped rice at 0.94 ppm and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.45 ppm. Against 0.45 ppm for the control, 8 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia was the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 0.18 and 0.45 ppm, with the control at 0.19 ppm. 8 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Gobindabhog ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 0.38 in Lal Badshabhog to 0.84 ppm in Kalonunia. The control recorded 0.43 ppm, 6 cultivars exceeded the control, and Kalonunia gave the most favourable value. Table 4.84 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.45. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. Significance attached to year in 3 products and to the year by cultivar interaction in 1, leaving cultivar ranking broadly unchanged from year to year. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 4.30 to 5.96%.

Manganese enters through NRAMP and MTP transporters and accumulates in the aleurone, so the value depends on uptake and on how much of the outer grain survives milling. Similar results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) recorded aleurone bound elements are displaced as water redistributes, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed soluble minerals migrate inward during steeping. Sonu et al. (2025) noted genotype counts for more than environment in mineral density, Kumar et al. (2022) concluded retention depends on the starting level and the treatment.
Gobindabhog and Kalonunia each headed the ranking in a different product, so this attribute cannot settle the selection for the group as a whole.

Lightness measures how pale the product has remained. It falls with browning and with inward movement of pigments, so a higher value generally indicates gentler processing. For popped rice the values lay between 64.32 and 72.78, with the control at 69.97. 4 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog being the highest among them. In puffed rice the values ranged from 67.79 in Tulaipanji to 75.51 in Kataribhog. Against the control at 72.23, 4 cultivars ranked higher, Kataribhog being the highest. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 77.35 and Kalojira the lowest at 69.63. Against 77.35 for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. The data are presented in Table 4.85 and plotted in Fig. 4.46.

The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. The year effect was significant in 2 products, but the interaction was not significant anywhere, so the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.04 and 0.39%, so the trial was precise. Lightness falls as browning products accumulate and as pericarp pigments dissolve and migrate inward. Cultivars with more reducing sugar and free amino nitrogen brown further under the same treatment.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated darkening comes from pigment movement and browning, Srisang et al. (2021) found lightness falls as the thermal treatment becomes harsher. Panda et al. (2021) reported shorter heating gives a lighter product at the same moisture loss, Akter et al. (2025) observed a darker product was still preferred overall. No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Dudeshwar and Kataribhog ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

The a* value is signed: a positive value places the sample on the red side of the green to red axis and a negative value on the green side. Redness increases as browning proceeds, so a lower value is preferred. In popped rice the values ranged from -1.86 in Radhatilak to 1.47 in Tulaipanji. The control recorded -0.90, 2 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhatilak gave the most favourable value. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.55 and Harinakhuri the lowest at -1.40. Against -0.72 for the control, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Harinakhuri was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between -1.03 and 1.50, with the control at -0.53. 3 cultivars exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked first. Table 4.86 lists the means and Fig. 4.47 presents them graphically. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. The year effect was significant in 1 product, but the interaction was not significant anywhere, so the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from -4.61 to 11.92%, indicating good experimental precision.

Redness rises as melanoidins and their coloured precursors accumulate, and the rate depends on the reducing sugars and free amino acids the cultivar supplies. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded the amber shift comes from Maillard browning, Srisang et al. (2021) showed colour builds with time and temperature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) noted how far colour develops is cultivar specific, Panda et al. (2021) concluded shorter heating limits colour development.
The most favourable entry differed between products. Harinakhuri and Radhatilak each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Yellowness arises from bran pigments migrating into the endosperm and from early browning products. Except where a golden colour is required, a lower value is better. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in popped rice at 114.00 and Tulaipanji the lowest at 101.07. The control recorded 108.11. 4 cultivars exceeded it and Tulaipanji ranked most favourable. For puffed rice the values lay between 6.13 and 12.09, with the control at 8.65. Here 3 cultivars exceeded the control, with Radhatilak the highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 7.62 in Tulaipanji to 11.62 in Kalonunia. The control gave 9.49; 5 cultivars exceeded that value and Tulaipanji ranked first. The means are given in Table 4.87 and plotted in Fig. 4.48.

Significance was reached in each of the products. In 1 products the year effect was significant and in 1 the year by cultivar interaction, so the cultivars kept similar order in both years. The coefficient of variation ran from 0.28 to 3.18%, which points to reliable measurement. Yellowness arises from carotenoids and flavonoids carried in from the pericarp during hydration together with early browning products, so cultivars with more pigment give higher values.

Published work agrees. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated bran pigments dissolve on soaking and fix on drying, Srisang et al. (2021) found yellowing is proportional to the heat load. Devi and Badwaik (2022) reported colour readings track pigment composition, Oliveira et al. (2026) observed final colour depends on pigment and on processing together. The leading cultivar changed with the product, Radhatilak and Tulaipanji ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

This measures the overall colour distance between the product and the raw grain. A smaller value means the grain has changed in texture without changing greatly in appearance. For popped rice the values lay between 33.99 and 45.45, with the control at 38.86. Tulaipanji ranked first, and 4 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In puffed rice the values ranged from 35.73 in Kataribhog to 44.73 in Tulaipanji. With the control at 43.67, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Kataribhog was the best. Tulaipanji recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 45.97 and Kataribhog the lowest at 36.05. Against 44.27 for the control, 6 cultivars exceeded it, and Kataribhog was the most favourable entry. Table 4.88 gives the means and Fig. 4.49 shows them. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was measured. The year term was significant in 2 products and the year by cultivar term in 1, so cultivar ranking held fairly steady between years. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation falling between 0.56 and 0.67%.

This combines all three colour coordinates and so registers both pigment migration and browning, each of which scales with what the cultivar provides. Previous reports run along the same lines. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded colour is the main barrier to accepting processed rice, Srisang et al. (2021) showed a combined colour index separates treatments better than one axis. Panda et al. (2021) noted the same processing can be had at a smaller colour cost, Akter et al. (2025) concluded overall colour change matched what the panel judged.
The leading position was shared between Kataribhog and Tulaipanji, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

Aroma distinguishes the traditional aromatic cultivars from ordinary grain and arises mainly from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. A higher score is clearly better. In popped rice the values ranged from 5.98 in Dudeshwar to 8.59 in Kalojira. The control recorded 5.98, 9 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalojira was the most favourable. Kalojira recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 7.99 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 3.98. The control gave 3.98; 9 cultivars exceeded it, Kalojira most markedly. For flattened rice the values lay between 4.14 and 6.96, with the control at 4.14. 9 of the cultivars exceeded the control; Kalojira ranked highest. The values appear in Table 4.89, with Fig. 4.50 showing the same data.

Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Year and its interaction with cultivar both fell short of significance, so the order was the same in each year. With coefficients of variation of 3.08 to 5.26%, the experiment was well controlled. Aroma arises mainly from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, which accumulates when the BADH2 gene is non functional and its precursor is free to cyclise. The compound is volatile, so thermal exposure also matters.

Published work points in the same direction. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) demonstrated sensory character shifts with treatment in a cultivar specific way, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) found over processing gives off odours through lipid oxidation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) reported aroma is one of the attributes traditional products are graded on, Panda et al. (2021) observed shorter heating keeps more of the volatiles. Kalojira gave the most favourable value in every product of this group, and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

Flavour combines aroma, taste and mouthfeel, and is among the strongest determinants of whether a product is accepted or rejected. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in popped rice at 8.68 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.03. Relative to 6.03 for the control, 9 cultivars were higher, with Radhunipagal the best among them. For puffed rice the values lay between 5.98 and 6.95, with the control at 6.53. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Radhatilak ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 4.10 in Dudeshwar to 7.14 in Harinakhuri. Against the control at 4.10, 9 cultivars ranked higher, Harinakhuri being the highest. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.90 and illustrated in Fig. 4.51. The cultivars were significantly different in every product. Neither year nor the year by cultivar term reached significance; ranking was unchanged between years. The coefficient of variation stayed within 2.49 to 4.43%, a sign of good precision.

Flavour combines the volatile fraction with the sugars and amino acids released on cooking and with the texture of the grain, so cultivars strong in aroma and moderate in firmness score well. The same pattern has been reported before. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) recorded flavour responds to processing more sensitively than instruments do, Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) showed flavour improves with firmer texture until treatment goes too far. Roy et al. (2019) noted flavour moves with the bioactive and physicochemical properties, Akter et al. (2025) concluded flavour and texture outweighed colour in overall liking.
No single cultivar was superior in all the products. Harinakhuri, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal ranked highest in different ones, so the decision depends on the product concerned.

Appearance governs the first impression and therefore whether the product is tried at all. For popped rice the values lay between 5.95 and 7.13, with the control at 6.42. 2 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog being the highest among them. In puffed rice the values ranged from 5.91 in Lal Badshabhog to 8.47 in Dudeshwar. The control recorded 8.47, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar gave the most favourable value. Harinakhuri recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 7.91 and Tulaipanji the lowest at 6.32. The control recorded 6.72. 3 cultivars exceeded it and Harinakhuri ranked most favourable. Table 4.91 carries the means; they are drawn in Fig. 4.52.

The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. No significance attached to year or to its interaction with cultivar, and the order stood in both seasons. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 2.27 to 5.01%. Appearance follows the colour coordinates, which are determined by pigment migration and browning, so the cultivars that remain pale head the ranking.

Earlier reports support this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated colour is among the two attributes that most limit acceptance, Dutta and Mahanta (2014) found appearance caps the market whatever the nutritional merit. Srisang et al. (2021) reported harder processing gives a visibly darker product, Akter et al. (2025) observed a darker product was nonetheless more acceptable overall. The most favourable entry differed between products. Dudeshwar, Harinakhuri and Kataribhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so the selection depends on the product concerned.

Consistency describes the textural coherence of the finished dish and how well it matches what the preparation requires. In popped rice the values ranged from 5.99 in Radhunipagal to 7.21 in Kataribhog. The control recorded 6.56, one cultivar exceeded the control, and Kataribhog gave the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 8.52 and Kalojira the lowest at 5.76. Against 8.52 for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 6.25 and 7.71, with the control at 6.70. Here one cultivar exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked highest. The data are presented in Table 4.92 and plotted in Fig. 4.53. All the products showed a significant cultivar effect. The year effect was not significant in any product, though the year by cultivar interaction was significant in 1, so in that product the difference between cultivars was not of the same magnitude in both years. Coefficients of variation lay between 3.58 and 4.03%, so the trial was precise.

Consistency depends on the degree of starch gelatinisation and subsequent retrogradation, and on the protein network surrounding the granules. Similar results have been published elsewhere. Cheng et al. (2019) recorded heat and moisture give a firmer, less sticky network, Iqbal et al. (2021) showed firmness follows the starch and protein network. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) noted texture and colour together decide acceptance, Devi and Badwaik (2022) concluded texture and pasting follow amylose and starch structure.
The leading cultivar changed with the product, Dudeshwar, Harinakhuri and Kataribhog ranking highest in turn, so no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Cooking quality summarises water uptake, cooking time and the structural integrity of the cooked grain. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in popped rice at 7.07 and Lal Badshabhog the lowest at 6.08. Against 6.56 for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Gobindabhog was the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 6.00 and 8.44, with the control at 8.44. Here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 6.12 in Tulaipanji to 7.56 in Harinakhuri. The control gave 6.57; 2 cultivars exceeded that value and Harinakhuri ranked first. Table 4.93 lists the means and Fig. 4.54 presents them graphically.

Significance was reached in each of the products. Year had no significant effect, alone or in combination with cultivar, so the ranking repeated. The coefficient of variation ran from 3.58 to 4.05%, which points to reliable measurement. Cooking quality depends on gelatinisation temperature, amylose content and the structural integrity of the grain, which is why it tracks alkali spreading value and amylose.

Comparable observations appear in the literature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) demonstrated cooking behaviour changes steadily with treatment severity, Kwofie and Ngadi (2017) found time and temperature are the processor's main control. Buggenhout et al. (2013) reported cultivar and processing history act together, Cheng et al. (2019) observed gelatinisation governs water uptake and cooking time. The leading position was shared between Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog and Harinakhuri, so the selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

The analysis of variance answers one attribute at a time, so a single figure was needed to establish which cultivar is best overall. This was done using the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), where each attribute is scored, weighted for its importance, and the weighted scores summed. Kraggerud et al. (2012) later examined whether such a score genuinely reflects overall quality and concluded that it does. Here every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was put on a scale of 0 to 100, oriented so that 100 always denotes the better outcome, then averaged within five groups and combined by weight: sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. The weights are a stated convention rather than a property of the data, and the index may be recomputed under any alternative set. The result is given in Table 4.94, and the score of every cultivar in every group appears in Table 4.96.

On this index the best cultivar was Gobindabhog for popped rice; Radhatilak for puffed rice; Harinakhuri for flattened rice. The control came at or near the bottom in every product, so replacing Dudeshwar with the cultivars named here would improve the product without any change in the method of preparation. Table 4.95 gives, for each product, the cultivar with the best balance of attributes against the control.

The table below gives the five group scores and the composite score for every cultivar in every product, so the standing of any entry may be read directly. The weights applied were sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.

sec: 4.29 Verification of the weights using principal component analysis (Part B)
text: The weights above were chosen rather than calculated, so the ranking was checked against a second set of weights taken from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was run on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading times the share of variance that component carries. It is the usual way of setting weights for a composite indicator without judgement. The two rankings agreed closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.952 and a lowest value of 0.939, and the same cultivar came first in 3 of the 3 products, as Table 4.97 shows. The ranking therefore follows from the data and not from the particular weights chosen. Principal component analysis is used here only to set the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, because a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the better one.

sec: 4.29 Verification of the weights using principal component analysis (Part B)
text: The mean rank correlation was 0.952 and the lowest 0.939, and the same cultivar came first in 3 of the 3 products. The ranking is therefore not an artefact of the weights chosen. Where the two disagreed, the cultivars concerned were close together on the index in any case, so the disagreement is one of order between near equals rather than of substance.

Cluster analysis was used to examine how the cultivars and the products group together when all the attributes are considered simultaneously. The 30 cultivar and product combinations were standardised on the 22 attributes measured in every product, and Ward's method was applied to the Euclidean distances between them. The number of groups was set at 3. Where a cluster contains only one product, it is the method of preparation that determines the quality profile; where cultivars of different products fall together, the two are comparable in the finished form.

Of the 3 clusters, 2 contain only one product. This indicates that the products differ from one another more than the cultivars differ within any one product. Amarnath and Ravi Kumar (2025) used Ward's method in the same way in rice and drew on the cluster means to pick genotypes for further work, on the reasoning that crosses between distant clusters are more likely to give useful variation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) made the same point from the product side, that different traditional preparations need genuinely different raw material.

Nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal were tested against Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar used as the control, in the 3 processed products of this group. Each was grown and prepared in the same way for two years and analysed as a pooled completely randomised design. In every product the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes measured, while the year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for far fewer. The main finding is therefore straightforward: the choice of cultivar determines the quality of the product, and the year of production makes much less difference. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally hold its position in the next.

On this index the best cultivar was Gobindabhog for popped rice; Radhatilak for puffed rice; Harinakhuri for flattened rice. The control came at or near the bottom in every product, so replacing Dudeshwar with the cultivars named here would improve the product without any change in the method of preparation. Table 4.95 gives, for each product, the cultivar with the best balance of attributes against the control.

The weights above were chosen rather than calculated, so the ranking was checked against a second set of weights taken from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was run on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading times the share of variance that component carries. That is the usual way of setting weights for a composite indicator without judgement. The two rankings agreed closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.952 and a lowest value of 0.939, and the same cultivar came first in 3 of the 3 products, as Table 4.97 shows. The ranking therefore follows from the data and not from the particular weights chosen. Principal component analysis is used here only to set the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, because a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the better one.

Cluster analysis was then run on all 30 cultivar and product combinations together, using the 22 attributes measured in every product. Ward's method placed them in 3 groups, of which 2 contained a single product only (Table 4.98 and Fig. 4.55). When the products are compared with one another, therefore, it is the method of preparation rather than the cultivar that determines the broad quality type, whereas within any one product the cultivar is the variable under the control of the processor. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory: the preparation determines the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.

The cultivars named here should be tested again on a larger scale and over more years before being recommended generally. For breeding work aimed at improving the group as a whole, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are more likely to release useful variation.

Across the seven products of this experiment the cultivars differed significantly for nearly every attribute measured, while the year of production and its interaction with cultivar were significant for far fewer. The choice of cultivar therefore governs the quality of the finished product, and the year in which the crop was grown makes much less difference. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally hold its position in the next.

On the composite quality score index the best cultivar was Gobindabhog for payash, popped rice; Kalojira for table rice; Radhunipagal for khichdi; Kataribhog for pulao; Radhatilak for puffed rice; Harinakhuri for flattened rice. In every product the non-aromatic control ranked at or near the foot of the order, so replacing Dudeshwar with the cultivars named here would improve the product without any change in the method of preparation. No single cultivar was best for all seven products, which means the choice of raw material has to follow the product intended.

The weights used in the index were chosen rather than calculated, so the ranking was checked against weights derived from a principal component analysis of the merit scores. Taking the seven products together, the mean rank correlation between the two was 0.946 and the same cultivar came first in 6 of the seven. The ranking is therefore a property of the data rather than of the weights adopted.

Cluster analysis of the cultivar and product combinations gave 7 groups across the two parts, of which 5 held a single product only. Comparing one preparation with another, it is the method of preparation rather than the cultivar that determines the broad quality type; within any one preparation the cultivar is the variable under the control of the processor. The preparation therefore fixes the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.

The cultivars identified here should be tested again on a larger scale and over more years before any general recommendation is made. For breeding aimed at improving the group as a whole, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are more likely to release useful variation.

This experiment was carried out to study the sensory and nutritional quality of idli prepared from three aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal and one non-aromatic control. The experiment was laid out in a two factor completely randomised design with three replications and was repeated in two years. Factor A was the variety, namely Gobindabhog (G), Radhunipagal (R), Kalojira (K) and the non-aromatic control Dudeshwar (D). Factor B was the product, namely plain idli (I), idli fortified with carrot extract (CI) and idli fortified with beet extract (BI). This gave twelve treatment combinations, which are written as DBI, DCI, DI, GBI, GCI, GI, KBI, KCI, KI, RBI, RCI and RI. The results are presented and discussed below.

sec: 4.33 Design of the experiment and pooling of the data
text: The two years of data were combined only after testing the error variances by the Bartlett chi-square test (Gomez and Gomez, 1984). The test was not significant for most characters, which showed that the error variances of the two years were similar and that the data could be pooled. It was significant only for manganese, ash, PGI and springiness. For these four characters an Aitken transformation was applied before the analysis of variance and the transformed means were used for testing significance (Panse and Sukhatme, 1985).

sec: 4.33 Design of the experiment and pooling of the data
text: The experiment was precise. The coefficient of variation was below 3% for most characters and was lowest for calcium (0.20%), total phenol and total antioxidant activity (0.34% each). It was higher for fat (15.91%), resilience (11.71%), copper (9.65%) and anthocyanin (9.63%). Higher values are expected for constituents present in small amounts and measured after extraction (Das and Giri, 1986).

sec: 4.33 Design of the experiment and pooling of the data
text: The variety and product interaction was highly significant for most of the nutritional, mineral, colour and textural characters. This means that the four varieties did not respond in the same way to fortification. The interaction was not significant only for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability.

sec: 4.33 Design of the experiment and pooling of the data
text: In the tables that follow, the values of the two years and the pooled value of the twelve treatment combinations are given as mean plus or minus standard deviation. The year values are means of three replications and the pooled values are means of six observations. The standard error of the mean, the critical difference at the 5% level and the coefficient of variation are given below each table. Pooled means followed by the same letter do not differ significantly at the 5% level. Each table is followed by a figure showing the pooled means, in which the vertical bars are the standard error of the mean and the letters above the bars are the groupings at the 5% level.

Amylose decides the cooking and eating quality of rice products because it controls how much the starch retrogrades on cooling, and therefore how firm or sticky the product becomes (Juliano, 1992; Tester et al., 2004). Amylose ranged from 16.75% in DI to 9.78% in RBI (Table 4.99). DI was at par with KI (16.25%). All twelve combinations fall in the low amylose group of Juliano (1992). This explains the soft and moist texture of idli made from these small grained landraces (Singh et al., 2000). Within each variety, amylose fell from the plain product to the carrot fortified and then to the beet fortified product. The size of this fall differed between varieties, which is why the interaction was significant.
