Starch showed the same pattern and ranged from 51.66% in DI to 24.05% in GBI (Table 4.100). Total carbohydrate ranged from 60.21% in DI to 40.91% in KBI (Table 4.101). Two reasons explain the fall in the fortified treatments. First, the vegetable extract dilutes the rice and black gram base (Sharma et al., 2012; Chhikara et al., 2019). Second, the amylolytic microflora of the batter breaks down a part of the starch during fermentation (Steinkraus, 1996; Nout, 2009). The non-aromatic control gave higher starch and carbohydrate than the aromatic landraces, which agrees with Verma and Srivastav (2017).

Total soluble sugar behaved in the opposite way and rose from 0.53% in RI to 3.83% in RBI (Table 4.102). Beetroot is rich in free sugars (Singh and Hathan, 2014) and the amylases of the fermenting microflora release further reducing sugars from the rice starch (Blandino et al., 2003).

Resistant starch is the fraction that escapes digestion in the small intestine and is fermented in the colon (Englyst et al., 1992; Sajilata et al., 2006). It ranged from 1.97% in DCI to 1.02% in KBI (Table 4.103) and non-resistant starch from 50.78% in DI to 23.57% in GBI (Table 4.104). The carrot fortified treatments gave the highest resistant starch. This is because carrot adds dietary fibre, and because amylose retrogrades when the steamed product cools and forms the RS3 fraction (Sajilata et al., 2006).

The predicted glycaemic index, worked out by the in vitro method of Goñi et al. (1997), ranged from 58.46 in RCI to 75.08 in KBI (Table 4.105). Treatments with more resistant starch gave a lower glycaemic index. This confirms the finding of Frei et al. (2003) that the resistant fraction, and not the total starch, decides the glycaemic response of rice foods. Carrot fortification is therefore better than beet fortification when a low glycaemic product is wanted, because carrot fibre slows enzyme access to the starch granule (Sharma et al., 2012).

Total soluble protein, estimated by the method of Lowry et al. (1951), ranged from 2.71% in KBI to 1.05% in DI (Table 4.106). Total protein ranged from 13.44% in KI to 10.92% in DCI (Table 4.107). The idli was richer in protein than milled rice for two reasons. The black gram in the batter supplies lysine rich protein that makes up for the lysine poor protein of rice (Reddy et al., 1981; Ufaz and Galili, 2008), and fermentation adds protein through microbial growth and proteolysis (Chavan and Kadam, 1989; Ghosh and Chattopadhyay, 2011). The aromatic landraces gave more protein than the control, and Radhunipagal combined high protein with low amylose. This agrees with the negative relation between grain protein and amylose reported by Chattopadhyay et al. (2018).

Fat was low in all treatments, as expected for a steamed product, and ranged from 0.28% in KI and GCI to 0.17% in GBI and RBI (Table 4.108). The carrot fortified treatments were slightly higher because the carotenoids of carrot are extracted along with the fat during Soxhlet extraction (Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001). Ash ranged from 5.21% in GBI to 2.47% in DI (Table 4.109) and was highest in the beet fortified treatment of every variety, since beetroot adds a good quantity of minerals (Chhikara et al., 2019).

Phytate is the main anti-nutritional factor of cereal and pulse foods because it binds divalent cations and makes them unavailable (Reddy et al., 1982; Haug and Lantzsch, 1983). It ranged from 2.52 mg g⁻¹ in KBI to 0.82 mg g⁻¹ in GI (Table 4.110) and was highest in the beet fortified treatments. All values were much lower than those normally reported for raw rice and black gram, because phytase from the grain and from the microflora breaks down phytate during soaking and fermentation (Lestienne et al., 2005; Gupta et al., 2015). The mineral gain from fortification is therefore partly cancelled by a rise in phytate. What matters for absorption is the phytate to mineral ratio and not the mineral content alone (Hemalatha et al., 2007).

The lower predicted glycaemic index of the carrot-fortified idli agrees with recent work on fibre-rich substitution in the same food. Sajayan et al. (2024) replaced part of the rice in idli batter with dried jackfruit bulb and recorded a lower starch hydrolysis index together with higher radical-scavenging activity and a larger lactic acid bacterial population, without loss of acceptability at moderate levels. Beetroot behaves in the same way in other cereal foods: Mitrevski et al. (2025) found that biscuits with 20% beetroot powder had a glycaemic index of 49 and carried more potassium, phosphorus, zinc and betaine than the control while remaining the most preferred sample in sensory tests.

The interaction was highly significant for all the bioactive fractions, and Kalojira with beet extract was the best combination for each of them. Total phenol, measured by the Folin-Ciocalteu method (Kaur and Kapoor, 2002), ranged from 290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in KBI to 53.47 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in DI (Table 4.111), a difference of more than five times. Total flavonoid, measured by the aluminium chloride method (Chang et al., 2002), ranged from 171.34 to 42.95 mg QE 100 g⁻¹ (Table 4.112) and total antioxidant activity from 426.88 to 165.26 mg TE 100 g⁻¹ (Table 4.113).

Two things caused this variation. The first is the variety. Pigmented rice grains hold much more phenolic acid and flavonoid than white grains, and the pericarp of black rice is especially rich in them (Zhang et al., 2010; Sompong et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2014). Goufo and Trindade (2014) also reported that the antioxidant capacity of rice comes mainly from the bound phenolics of the bran layer. That is why the black husked Kalojira stayed ahead in every product form. The higher secondary metabolite content of aromatic landraces compared with non-aromatic types (Ghosh and Roychoudhury, 2018) was also clear in the present data.

The second is the fortifying material. Beetroot is one of the richest sources of betalain pigments and also carries phenolic acids (Ravichandran et al., 2013; Chhikara et al., 2019). Betalains are fairly stable at the mildly acidic pH produced by lactic fermentation, so most of the added pigment survived steaming. For this reason the beet fortified treatments were consistently high in phenol and antioxidant activity. The size of the gain differed between varieties, which explains the significant interaction.

Beta-carotene came almost entirely from carrot. It ranged from 45.77 in KCI and 43.59 in GCI to nil in every plain treatment (Table 4.114). Carrot is among the richest sources of provitamin A carotenoids, and its all-trans β-carotene is well retained under moist heat such as steaming, unlike frying or long dry heating (Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). Anthocyanin showed the opposite pattern and was found only in the beet fortified treatments, from 1.86 in KBI to 0.98 in DBI (Table 4.115). It comes from the betacyanin of beetroot together with pigment carried over from the black husk of Kalojira (Sompong et al., 2011). KCI can therefore be used for a provitamin A rich product and KBI for an anthocyanin rich product (Bagchi et al., 2020).

The interaction was significant for all five minerals. Copper ranged from 0.97 ppm in GBI to 0.21 ppm in KCI and DI (Table 4.116) and iron from 3.36 ppm in RI to 1.36 ppm in DI (Table 4.117). Zinc ranged from 0.89 ppm in RI to 0.64 ppm in DI (Table 4.118) and manganese from 0.69 ppm in GI to 0.37 ppm in DI (Table 4.119). Manganese is worth noting because the interaction was significant even though the main effect of fortification was not, which shows that the response to the extract depended on the variety.

Calcium varied most widely, from 550.88 ppm in GBI to 61.44 ppm in KI (Table 4.120). The beet fortified treatment was highest in every variety, followed by the carrot fortified treatment. Beetroot is a useful source of calcium and other minerals for cereal foods (Chhikara et al., 2019). This gain is important because rice based diets are poor in calcium (Rani et al., 2006).

The mineral results must be read together with the phytate values. Phytate binds calcium, iron and zinc in the gut and forms complexes that are poorly absorbed, and a phytate to zinc molar ratio above fifteen indicates poor zinc availability (Reddy et al., 1982; Hemalatha et al., 2007). Soaking and fermentation activate phytase and remove a good part of the phytate, which improves the availability of iron and zinc in the finished product (Lestienne et al., 2005; Gupta et al., 2015). Among the twelve combinations, the plain and carrot fortified treatments of Gobindabhog combined good mineral content with low phytate and are therefore the best from the point of view of mineral availability.

The rise in calcium and other minerals with beet fortification matches the mineral enrichment that Mitrevski et al. (2025) reported for beetroot powder in a cereal product, where potassium, phosphorus and zinc all increased with the level of addition.

Colour is the first thing a consumer notices and it strongly affects the acceptance of a fermented cereal product (Amerine et al., 1965; Pathare et al., 2013). Lightness ranged from 72.92 in DI to 36.47 in DBI (Table 4.121). Within every variety it fell in the order plain, carrot fortified, beet fortified. Redness rose from -1.81 in DI to 13.26 in DCI (Table 4.122) and yellowness fell from 110.98 in DI to 59.45 in DBI (Table 4.123).

The total colour difference ranged from 45.02 in RCI to 28.70 in RI (Table 4.124). These values are far above the threshold of about three units at which a colour change becomes visible to an untrained eye (Pathare et al., 2013). The hue angle moved from -90.21 in GI towards the red region in the fortified treatments (Table 4.125), and chroma fell from 110.83 in DI to 59.72 in DBI (Table 4.126), showing that the fortified products were darker but not less saturated.

These changes follow from the pigment chemistry of the two vegetables. The betacyanin of beetroot gives an intense red to violet colour that is fairly stable at the mildly acidic pH of the fermented batter and survives short steaming, though it breaks down under long or dry heating (Ravichandran et al., 2013; Chhikara et al., 2019). The carotenoids of carrot give an orange to yellow colour, are more heat stable, and raise redness without lowering lightness as much (Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). Kalojira gave a darker product in every form because of pigment carried over from the black husk (Sompong et al., 2011). The high appearance scores of the fortified products, discussed later, show that the panel liked this colour change.

The texture of idli depends on how well the fermented batter holds gas, which in turn depends on the interaction between the globulin and arabinogalactan of black gram and the gelatinised starch of rice (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005). Hardness ranged from 147.73 in KI to 45.09 in DI (Table 4.127). The plain product was the hardest in every variety, which shows that adding a vegetable extract dilutes the starch and protein network and gives a more tender product.

Adhesiveness was least negative in DI (-0.19) and most negative in RI (-19.58) (Table 4.128). Springiness ranged from 1.04 in DI to 0.46 in KBI (Table 4.129), cohesiveness from 0.94 in KI to 0.40 in KBI (Table 4.130) and resilience from 0.55 in GI to 0.19 in RBI (Table 4.133). Gumminess and chewiness are calculated from hardness and cohesiveness (Bourne, 2002), so they followed the same pattern, with the highest values of 11890.93 and 10263.60 in KI (Tables 4.131 and 4.132) and the lowest in KBI.

The link between amylose and hardness is worth noting. The plain treatments had the most amylose and were also the hardest and most cohesive. This is because amylose retrogrades and forms a firm gel network as the product cools (Tester et al., 2004; Mohapatra and Bal, 2006). The fortified treatments, in which amylose was diluted, gave a softer and less chewy product. These instrumental values match the texture scores given by the panel, which supports the view of Szczesniak (2002) that instrumental texture analysis of a steamed cereal product agrees well with panel judgement.

The sensory data were recorded by a semi-trained panel on a nine point hedonic scale following Amerine et al. (1965) and Meilgaard et al. (2007). Aroma was highest in GI (7.70), which was at par with GCI (7.25), and lowest in KCI (5.65) and DI (5.72) (Table 4.134). This shows that the aroma of the landraces, which comes mainly from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (Buttery et al., 1983; Bhattacharjee et al., 2002), survives soaking, grinding, fermentation and steaming. The lower aroma scores of the fortified treatments within each aromatic variety show that the vegetable extract partly masks the natural aroma of the rice, even though it improves colour and taste (Ghosh and Roychoudhury, 2018).

Flavour showed a significant interaction and ranged from 7.96 in KBI to 5.46 in DI (Table 4.136). The interaction was not significant for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability (Tables 4.135, 4.137 to 4.140). Here is an important finding, because it means the sensory gain from fortification was the same in all four varieties and is not limited to any one landrace. Overall acceptability was highest in KBI (8.64), followed by KCI (8.24), and lowest in DI (6.14).

The higher scores of the fortified treatments for appearance and overall acceptability follow from the colour results, since a natural pigment greatly improves the look of a white steamed product (Pathare et al., 2013). The higher texture scores follow from the instrumental data, as the panel preferred the softer and less chewy products. Similar gains in consumer preference after adding pigment rich cereal and vegetable fractions to traditional Indian foods have been reported by Pal et al. (2019) and Bagchi et al. (2020). The present results show that the aromatic landraces of West Bengal can be made into an attractive and nutritionally better fermented food without any synthetic colour or additive.

The relations among the forty two quality parameters were studied by working out the Pearson correlation coefficient over twenty four treatment means, that is the twelve treatment combinations in each of the two years. The full correlation matrix is shown as a heat map in Fig. 4.98 and the correlation of overall acceptability with every other parameter is given in Table 4.141. At twenty two degrees of freedom the critical values of r are 0.404 at the 5% level and 0.515 at the 1% level (Snedecor and Cochran, 1994).

The three bioactive fractions were closely related. Total phenol was correlated with total flavonoid (r = 0.983) and with total antioxidant activity (r = 0.971), and total flavonoid with total antioxidant activity (r = 0.945). All three were significant at the 1% level. This shows that the antioxidant potential of the product comes almost entirely from its phenolic and flavonoid content, which agrees with Zhang et al. (2010), Sompong et al. (2011) and Goufo and Trindade (2014). Total soluble protein was also correlated with total phenol (r = 0.767) and phytate with total phenol (r = 0.632). Protein, phytate and bound phenolic acids all occur together in the aleurone and sub-aleurone layers of the grain (Reddy et al., 1982).

The carbohydrate fractions were negatively correlated with the bioactive fractions. Total carbohydrate was negatively correlated with total phenol (r = -0.913) and starch with total antioxidant activity (r = -0.955), both significant at the 1% level. Total carbohydrate was itself correlated with starch (r = 0.895) and amylose (r = 0.824), and lightness with yellowness (r = 0.995) and with total carbohydrate (r = 0.832). All these relations express one underlying gradient, namely the replacement of the starchy rice base by the pigment rich vegetable extract. Hence the fortified products were at the same time darker, lower in starch and richer in antioxidants.

Among the textural parameters, hardness was correlated with gumminess (r = 0.913) and chewiness (r = 0.816), as expected since both are calculated from hardness (Bourne, 2002). Springiness was correlated with amylose (r = 0.640) and cohesiveness with amylose (r = 0.484), which supports the view that the elastic recovery of the steamed product depends on the amylose network formed on cooling (Tester et al., 2004). Resistant starch was negatively correlated with the predicted glycaemic index (r = -0.587), which agrees with Frei et al. (2003) and Sajilata et al. (2006). Ash was correlated with calcium (r = 0.804), showing that the mineral load of the product was governed mainly by the calcium from the fortifying material.

Overall acceptability was negatively correlated with total carbohydrate (r = -0.895), non-resistant starch (r = -0.716), starch (r = -0.710), springiness (r = -0.691) and lightness (r = -0.662), and positively correlated with total flavonoid (r = 0.782), total antioxidant activity (r = 0.780), total phenol (r = 0.773), hue angle (r = 0.762), phytate (r = 0.753) and total soluble protein (r = 0.746). The panel therefore preferred the darker, less starchy, softer and more antioxidant rich products, which is exactly the profile of the fortified treatments. Aroma was the only sensory attribute not correlated with overall acceptability (r = -0.123). Aroma and general palatability were thus governed by different constituents, and a high aroma score alone did not give a high acceptability score.

Taste, flavour, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability were correlated with one another at unity in the present data, the six scores differing only by a constant. Their relations with the physico-chemical parameters are therefore identical, and only overall acceptability has been used in the multivariate analysis that follows.

Principal component analysis was carried out on the standardised values of the forty two parameters over the twenty four treatment means. The purpose was to reduce the number of dimensions and to find out which parameters contribute most to the variation among the treatment combinations (Jolliffe, 2002; Granato et al., 2018). The eigenvalues and variance explained by the first eight components are given in Table 4.142, the scree plot in Fig. 4.99, the loadings in Table 4.143 and the biplot of the first two components in Fig. 4.100.

Seven components had an eigenvalue above unity and were retained following Kaiser (1960). The first component alone explained 50.12% of the total variation and the second 14.12%, so the two together explained 64.24%. The first five components explained 86.66%. A first component of this size shows that one main gradient accounts for most of the variation among the twelve treatments.

The loadings in Table 4.143 identify this gradient clearly. The positive end of the first component was defined by total antioxidant activity (1.005), total phenol (0.968), total flavonoid (0.942), total soluble sugar (0.905) and overall acceptability (0.874). The negative end was defined by total carbohydrate (-0.988), non-resistant starch (-0.965), starch (-0.963), lightness (-0.927), yellowness (-0.893), chroma (-0.888), springiness (-0.875) and amylose (-0.836). The first component therefore separates the starchy, pale and firm plain products from the pigmented, antioxidant rich, soft and well liked fortified products. It can be called a fortification axis.

The second component was defined at its positive end by total protein (0.922), aroma (0.658), manganese (0.617), gumminess (0.608) and hardness (0.592), and at its negative end by resistant starch (-0.783), β-carotene (-0.644) and total colour difference (-0.590). This component separates the carrot fortified treatments, which were rich in β-carotene and resistant starch, from the plain and beet fortified treatments, which were higher in protein, aroma and firmness. It can be called a carrot fortification axis.

The biplot in Fig. 4.100 confirms these findings. The twelve treatments separated into three groups along the first component in the order plain, carrot fortified and beet fortified. Within each group the four varieties followed the order Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. KBI took the extreme positive position, close to the vectors of total phenol, total flavonoid, total antioxidant activity and anthocyanin, while DI took the extreme negative position, close to the vectors of total carbohydrate, starch and lightness. The two years of each treatment always fell close together, which shows graphically that the treatment effects were stable across years and that pooling was valid (Granato et al., 2018).

Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) prepared idli from pigmented rice cultivars of Tamil Nadu blended with pearl millet flour and found colour, texture and nutritional characters to differ significantly among the products, with insoluble-bound phenolics the dominant fraction and principal component analysis identifying the most promising formulations. The same approach, applied here to aromatic landraces and vegetable fortification, points to beetroot-fortified Kalojira idli.

Cluster analysis was carried out on the standardised values of the forty two parameters of the twelve treatment combinations in order to group the treatments by their overall quality. The squared Euclidean distance was used as the measure of dissimilarity and the groups were formed by the minimum variance method of Ward (1963), which is widely used for food quality data because it gives compact groups of nearly equal size (Everitt et al., 2011). The dendrogram is given in Fig. 4.101, the composition of the clusters in Table 4.144 and the cluster means in Table 4.145.

The cophenetic correlation coefficient was 0.793, which shows that the dendrogram represents the original distance matrix reasonably well (Murtagh and Legendre, 2014). The twelve treatments formed four clusters at a linkage distance of about 9.4. Cluster I contained the three plain products of the aromatic landraces, namely GI, KI and RI. Cluster II contained DI alone. Cluster III contained all four carrot fortified products and Cluster IV all four beet fortified products.

The important point about this grouping is that the first division was decided by fortification and not by variety. All four beet fortified treatments grouped together whatever the parent variety, and the same was true of the carrot fortified treatments. This confirms the result of the principal component analysis, namely that the type of fortification is the main source of variation in product quality. Variety mattered only at the second level, where the plain product of the non-aromatic control separated from the plain products of the three aromatic landraces and formed a cluster of its own. This separation of DI is itself useful, because it shows that the quality of the non-aromatic control differs from that of the aromatic landraces more than any two aromatic landraces differ from each other.

The cluster means in Table 4.145 describe the four groups. Cluster IV, the beet fortified group, had the highest total phenol (265.22 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹), total flavonoid (142.75 mg QE 100 g⁻¹), total antioxidant activity (393.44 mg TE 100 g⁻¹), total soluble protein (2.24%), calcium (500.89 ppm), anthocyanin (1.41) and overall acceptability (8.06), and the lowest amylose, starch, total carbohydrate and lightness. Cluster III, the carrot fortified group, was intermediate for the bioactive fractions but had by far the highest β-carotene (38.85), the highest resistant starch among the fortified groups (1.69%), the lowest predicted glycaemic index (60.49) and the highest redness (11.57). Cluster I, the plain aromatic group, had high starch, high total protein (13.09%), the greatest hardness (114.11) and a moderate acceptability of 7.28. Cluster II, made up of DI alone, had the highest amylose, starch and total carbohydrate and the lowest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity and overall acceptability (6.14).

The clustering thus supports the results of the analysis of variance and the principal component analysis. Cluster IV is the group of choice when a functional product of high antioxidant value and high acceptability is wanted, and Cluster III when a provitamin A rich product of low glycaemic response is wanted.

The results show that the variety, the type of fortification and their interaction all had a significant effect on the quality of idli made from aromatic rice. Fortification was the stronger of the two factors, and both the principal component analysis and the cluster analysis placed it, not variety, as the main source of variation.

The three aromatic landraces were better than the non-aromatic control Dudeshwar for protein, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant potential and every sensory attribute. Among them, Kalojira was richest in the bioactive fractions, Gobindabhog in minerals with the lowest phytate, and Radhunipagal gave the softest product. Beet extract raised phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, calcium and anthocyanin, while carrot extract supplied β-carotene and gave the highest resistant starch with the lowest glycaemic index. Both softened the product and improved its colour and acceptability, and the sensory gain was the same in all four varieties.

KBI is therefore recommended as the best combination, since it gave the highest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, soluble protein, anthocyanin and overall acceptability. KCI is suggested where a provitamin A rich product of low glycaemic response is wanted and GBI where a mineral enriched product is wanted. The study shows that the aromatic landraces of West Bengal can be made into an attractive and nutritionally improved fermented food using carrot and beet extract alone, without any synthetic colour or additive.
